Перед заявлением об улучшении выполнить:

```sh
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
npm run doctor
npm run bench
npm run benchmark:compare:check
npm run smoke:plugin
npm run smoke:package
npm run audit:dependencies
```

Дополнить актуальными host/native/installer-проверками при изменении адаптеров.
Обновить контракты инструментов, правила поведения модели, методологию
измерений и совместимость host-адаптеров. Результаты платных сравнений прилагать
отдельно: локальные проверки не заменяют измерение работы модели.

Итоговый принцип: Patchline должен экономить за счёт меньшего количества
ненужной работы, сохраняя проверки, которые защищают пользовательский код.

# Data Flow

Status: Accepted

## Read

`validate path -> read raw bytes -> decode -> snapshot -> select range -> render anchors`

## Edit

`validate scope -> load snapshot -> compare raw digest -> prepare in memory -> atomic replace -> invalidate -> diagnose`

## Multi-file edit

`validate all scopes -> validate all snapshots -> prepare all candidates -> preflight all writes -> commit with rollback data`

No source write occurs before path, scope, snapshot, and patch validation.
Existing-file replacements use a temporary file in the target directory followed by
an atomic entry replacement. Target and parent identities are rechecked before
temporary-file creation and again before rename; a swapped target or parent is
rejected and never followed. New-file creation remains exclusive (`wx`).

# Failure Model

Status: Accepted

Errors use stable codes and actionable messages. Safety errors are closed:
unknown encodings, workspace escapes, missing snapshots, scope mismatches, and
stale state prevent writes. Optional capability failures such as AST or LSP
unavailability return an explicit degraded result and do not weaken editing.
Hashline runtime unavailability follows the same rule: only the bounded linear
Node fallback is enabled, while unsupported structural or clipboard operations
fail closed.

Multi-file commit failures report landed paths and attempt byte-for-byte
rollback. Because portable filesystems cannot guarantee one atomic operation
across several paths, Patchline promises complete preflight and best-effort
rollback rather than claiming strict transactionality. Installer rollback also
captures local package manifests and lockfiles, restoring them only when their
current contents still reflect the failed installation; external changes are
reported as rollback conflicts. A landed write is tracked
before snapshot bookkeeping, so bookkeeping failures also enter guarded rollback.
The `writes` count records landed file writes, including those subsequently
restored; `details.restored` and `details.conflicts` describe rollback outcomes.
Exclusive creation is tracked as soon as the file is opened, before content,
verification, or close completes. Only confirmed written bytes and the captured
file identity authorize removal; missing identity or changed bytes are reported
as conflicts. Single-file creation uses the same guarded rollback and retains
pre-write safety error codes when no file was created.
Hashline removal/move retains the original file in a guarded temporary backup
until all commits succeed. Rollback restores through an exclusive hard link and
will not overwrite a recreated source or changed destination. Conflicted backups are
retained for recovery. Clipboard register state is published after successful
commit only. Mutation APIs propagate cancellation before preflight and between
commits; cancellation during a partial batch uses the same guarded rollback
and reports `cancelled`, `restored`, and `conflicts` metadata. Atomic replacement
cleanup after a successful rename is best-effort and cannot hide a landed write.
Snapshot and clipboard state is scoped to the session/worktree.

Installer mutations use a compensating transaction across configuration, owned
dependencies, LSP registration, and installer state. A failure restores
previous configuration and state when the files remain unchanged, and reports
rollback conflicts without overwriting external changes. Dependency cleanup is
scoped to the exact local or global installation that was changed.
Presentation callbacks cannot interrupt a commit or rollback. Post-edit validation
failures retain the applied diff, next snapshot and known write count.

# Module Map

Status: Accepted

| Module | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| `compatibility` | Runtime and dependency capability reports |
| `workspace` | Canonical paths, worktree identity, boundary enforcement |
| `preservation` | Raw UTF-8 bytes, BOM and line-ending round trips |
| `snapshot` | Session/worktree isolated observed-state history |
| `editing` | Exact edits, Hashline patches and multi-file preflight |
| `guards` | Existing-write, generated-file and unsafe-tool protection |
| `search` | Textual, structural and semantic routing |
| `validation` | Diagnostics and proportional command selection |
| `telemetry` | Local bounded event and task metrics |
| `tools` | OpenCode tool schemas and compact output formatting |

# Architecture

Status: Accepted

```text
OpenCode
  -> Patchline plugin
  -> guarded read/edit/write tools
  -> workspace resolver
  -> session-scoped snapshots
  -> anchored patch engine
  -> stale verification
  -> diagnostics and targeted validation
```

Patchline exposes a small model-facing surface. `read` records exactly the file
state shown to the model. `edit` verifies that state and applies either an
exact replacement or Hashline patch. `write` creates files but refuses to
replace existing source. Search providers are selected by intent: semantic
queries use native OpenCode LSP when enabled, text queries use grep, and syntax
queries use AST search.

Correctness is enforced below the model policy. Path boundaries, raw-content
digests, scope binding, and write protection remain active even if a model
uses the wrong tool.

# OpenCode Runtime Integration

Status: Accepted for OpenCode 1.18.30

Inspection was performed against installed OpenCode `1.18.30`,
`@opencode-ai/plugin@1.18.30`, and the matching `v1.18.30` source tag.

Confirmed integration points:

- `PluginInput` exposes `directory`, `worktree`, `project`, `client`, and shell.
- `ToolContext` exposes `sessionID`, `directory`, `worktree`, abort, metadata,
  and permission prompts.
- plugins may return a `tool` record and execution/system hooks;
- plugin tools are appended after built-ins and the final tool map is keyed by
  ID, so a same-ID plugin tool replaces the built-in model-facing definition;
- `tool.execute.before` runs before every selected tool and a thrown error
  prevents execution;
- built-in LSP is present but model-facing registration is gated by
  `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL` or the global experimental flag;
- current built-ins use IDs `read`, `edit`, `write`, `apply_patch`, and `lsp`.

Patchline therefore overrides `read`, `edit`, and `write`, registers explicit
additional tools, and also overrides `apply_patch`: OpenCode hides `edit` and
`write` for GPT model IDs and selects `apply_patch` instead. The Patchline
version accepts snapshot-tagged Hashline sections. The optional LSP bridge is
published as `patchline_lsp` so it does not mask OpenCode's native experimental
`lsp` tool. Unsafe fallback operations
remain guarded in the before hook. This behavior must be rechecked for each new
OpenCode minor line.

# Benchmark Methodology

Compare stock OpenCode, ordinary edit/apply_patch, and Patchline from identical
repository states with the same task, model, provider, and settings. Reset only
dedicated benchmark fixtures; never reset a user's working tree.

## Reproducible comparison

`npm run benchmark:compare:check` runs offline safety checks and all thirteen golden
solutions, then writes an autonomous Russian HTML report plus JSON, CSV and
Markdown under `benchmarks/reports/comparison/`. It makes no model requests.

Build the plugin first. A live pilot is **six sessions**, not six provider calls:

```sh
npm run build
npm run benchmark:compare -- run --stage pilot --max-sessions 6 --model provider/model --provider-config /path/to/opencode.json --stock-bin /path/to/upstream/opencode --patchline-bin /path/to/integrated/opencode --out benchmarks/reports/comparison-pilot
```

`--provider-config` is read as JSON/JSONC. Only the selected provider and selected
model are passed to isolated children. Currently the runner supports
`@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` with an explicit `options.baseURL` and `options.apiKey`.
Credentials are used in memory by the local relay and are not included in the
report. A local ephemeral relay requests `stream_options.include_usage` and records
actual streaming usage, response latency, request/response bytes and offered tool
names. It does not record provider messages or authentication headers. The relay
is bound to loopback; requests are forwarded to the configured provider.

Both binaries must have exactly the same upstream version; the stock binary must
not contain Patchline build metadata. Version strings and SHA-256 digests of both
binaries and the plugin are recorded. The intervention is **the complete installed
integration** (host tool selection plus plugin precision), not the plugin isolated
from its host changes. Same-model temperature 0 is requested; `--variant` can fix
the provider reasoning variant. Provider nondeterminism still applies.

Every session gets fresh fixture files, HOME/XDG locations and no inherited
`OPENCODE_*` flags. Project config, user plugins, MCP, instructions, title/summary
agents, LSP auto-install and formatting are disabled. A common prompt suffix and
permissions prevent subagents and unsolicited documentation. Hidden behavioral
checks execute after model completion outside its workspace. Timing includes CLI
startup and inference, excludes grading. Fresh dependency caches make startup part
of the measurement; provider caches cannot be flushed. Mode order alternates per
task/repeat. Each mode sees byte-identical starting files.

Defaults: 180 seconds/session, 16 agent steps and at most 19 provider requests via
the relay, including any retries. `--timeout` and `--steps` can change these bounds.
`--max-sessions` is mandatory for live runs. Full evaluation requires `--stage full
--max-sessions 130` (13 tasks × 2 modes × 5 repetitions). It is a separate explicit
invocation after reviewing pilot costs. No automatic expansion or paid retries.
If a session fails/times out, its consumed resources remain in the result.
Reports checkpoint after each session; existing source worktrees are never reset.
Use a new `--out` directory per experiment to preserve history.

```sh
npm run benchmark:compare:report -- --input benchmarks/reports/comparison-pilot/results.json --out benchmarks/reports/comparison-pilot
```

Use `--temp-root` to select an existing parent for disposable fixtures. Reports
contain fixture diffs and model/tool output; these are explicitly benchmark
artifacts, distinct from the content-free plugin telemetry contract.

Pilot results are descriptive only. The full series adds paired task-cluster
bootstrap intervals, not universal model-quality or release-performance claims.
There is no LLM judge or subjective style score. Inspect behavioral checks,
preservation and raw diffs together. No monetary savings are claimed without a
verified tariff; OpenCode cost zero can mean an unconfigured tariff.

Hidden checks require an explicit per-check completion marker in addition to a
successful process exit. An imported solution calling `process.exit(0)` before
assertions finish fails grading. The evaluator also compares workspace contents
before and after all checks; changes made during grading fail both functionality
and preservation. Unexpected additions in an intended file fail preservation,
even if behavioral assertions pass. These checks are integrity backstops, not an
OS sandbox: isolation of untrusted code and independent behavior observation
remain required before acceptance-quality comparisons.

Fixture contents are staged in a dedicated Git index before each session (with
automatic CRLF conversion disabled), so ordinary `git diff` sees modifications
and deletions against the initial bytes. No user repository is staged or reset.
Each paid run is persisted with `gradingStatus: pending` before hidden grading;
grader exceptions retain measurements and become explicit failed runs. A declared
task/repeat/mode manifest is saved before model requests. `integrity.complete`
requires every declared run exactly once, completed grading, and measured usage;
missing manifests, partial runs and duplicates cannot establish completeness.
File reads also verify lossless UTF-8 round trips; invalid bytes cannot masquerade
as preserved replacement characters after decoding, before or after grading.
Evaluation walks count directories and files before reading (500 entries,
32 levels), enforce 2 MB per file and 8 MB total, and reject non-regular entries.
Only the workspace's root `.git` metadata is excluded; nested `.git` names are
evaluated. Hidden-check children receive an allowlisted OS environment with
scratch HOME/TEMP, no inherited credentials or Node preload options, and bounded
execution through the process-tree timeout runner. This is still not an OS
sandbox or independent external assertion process.
Corpus behavior imports now use `vm.SourceTextModule` in a separate context,
with string/Wasm code generation disabled, no injected Node globals, and only
fixture-relative module linking. Assertions remain outside that context; tested
code cannot import and replace the checker's `node:assert`. This restricts direct
access but VM contexts are not a security boundary; an independently isolated
observation process remains required for acceptance of adversarial results.
HTML and Markdown explicitly mark missing/incomplete manifests as
`НЕПОЛНАЯ СЕРИЯ`, including reports whose requested stage is `full`.
Fixture Git removes inherited `GIT_*` overrides, disables global/system config and
attributes, uses an empty template, and persists `core.autocrlf=false` locally.
Provider measurements include a SHA-256 of the forwarded request and JSON byte
sizes per top-level section, without persisting request contents or credentials.
Diff precision now preserves CRLF/LF distinctions rather than normalizing them;
newline-only collateral changes therefore affect preservation on every task.
Preservation is evaluated separately from golden diff precision: task construction
declares editable regions from the requested replacements. All prefix, suffix
and intervening protected text must survive exactly and in order. Alternative
implementations inside those regions can pass behavioral checks without matching
the golden expression. Exact-byte tasks still require the unique requested bytes.
Before grading, each live attempt also writes a unique, exclusively created JSON
artifact containing redacted stdout/stderr and original measurements; its filename
and SHA-256 are linked from the run. Live provenance records corpus and lockfile
hashes plus the tracked source diff hash and dirty flag alongside binary/plugin
hashes. Before live model requests, the runner also copies current build inputs
into a temporary workspace, uses the installed toolchain to run `scripts/build.mjs`,
and compares every output path and byte against the measured `dist`. Missing,
extra or stale outputs fail the preflight. The measured source and distribution
are checked again after the rebuild; the measured tree is never rebuilt in place.
The matching source/distribution/rebuilt hashes are recorded as
`environment.reproducibleBuild`. This proves local reproducibility with the
installed toolchain, not independent trust in that toolchain.
Live provenance additionally fingerprints every file name and byte content under
`src`, `dist`, and the comparison harness, including untracked files, and records
installed TypeScript, OpenCode SDK/plugin, diff and Zod versions. Non-regular
source entries fail fingerprinting. A dirty-fixture regression verifies that
`git diff --check` detects introduced whitespace while pre-existing user edits and
the staged baseline remain intact.

Offline `check` records the same corpus SHA-256 and source/harness tree
fingerprints as live runs, including untracked source files. This associates
offline grading and replay evidence with the actual acceptance contract and
implementation used. Historical reports without these fields remain historical
evidence with unknown fingerprints; report regeneration must not attach current
fingerprints to their past executions. Offline checks do not claim a verified
distribution build unless separately measured.

Manifest integrity also rejects invalid session identities even when the same
invalid entry appears in both manifest and measured runs: task IDs must be
nonempty strings, repeats nonnegative safe integers, and modes `stock` or
`patchline`. Rejections are listed in `integrity.invalidIdentities` and prevent
`integrity.complete`. Identity validity does not by itself prove a balanced or
adequately powered experiment. Each declared task/repeat must include both modes;
missing counterparts are listed by task/repeat in `integrity.unpaired` and prevent
completeness even if every declared session was measured and graded. This checks
pair coverage, not the required task count or repetitions for a full experiment.

The live corpus now also includes `dirty-worktree`: its Git index is initialized
from a separate clean baseline before materializing pre-existing user edits.
Both modes see the same dirty target and unrelated notes file, and preservation
grading rejects loss of either user's content. This expands the full corpus to
13 tasks; older 12-task pilot projections do not describe the updated full run.
The full-series cost/time projection derives its session count from the current
corpus (task count × two modes × five repetitions), rather than a fixed 120.
Summary callers without an explicit projection size receive no projection.
Live CLI accepts the current full-series bound of 130 sessions and supports
`--tool-profile extended|compact` (default `extended`). The chosen profile is
passed only to Patchline plugin options and persisted as `report.toolProfile`;
stock remains plugin-free. Use a separate output directory for each profile.
Selecting a profile does not authorize or start a paid series by itself.

Offline `check` also records `batch-edit-replay`: the same two files and exact
edits are executed sequentially and as one atomic batch. Setup and snapshot
reads are excluded from timed mutation intervals. The first process-local pair
is separate from 20 warm pairs with alternating balanced order; each execution
must produce the exact expected bytes in both files. Reports retain raw pairs,
latency summaries and local mutation call counts (two versus one). These timings
include each service's safety work and do not imply provider token savings,
fewer model decisions, OS-cold behavior or superior failure recovery. Existing
stale/rollback tests remain independent safety evidence.

`report.toolProfiles` records deterministic per-tool JSON-schema byte sizes and
system-policy UTF-8 bytes for both plugin profiles with `lsp:false`. This is a
plugin-only local comparison: host-native tools, provider schema transformations,
tokenization and repeated request/caching costs are not included. Actual request
section byte counts continue to come from the relay during live runs.
The live runner fingerprints staged paths, modes, object IDs and `ls-files -v`
flags before and after each session. Missing/unreadable index state or changes
to that fingerprint fail the attempt even if functional grading passes. This
uses semantic staged state rather than raw index bytes, since ordinary Git
status refreshes can rewrite its stat cache. The before/after proof is stored
as `run.gitIndex` before grading.

Hidden behavioral checkers now run with Node's `--permission` model, allowing
filesystem reads only for the generated checker itself and granting no writes,
child processes, workers or addons. Fixture module bytes are embedded and still
loaded in the restricted VM context. The trusted `checkJs` action runs as a
separate permission-limited process, with read access only to the fixture and
installed TypeScript, and no child-process grant. Regression checks verify that
both in-fixture and out-of-fixture writes are denied without changing bytes.
The comparison evaluator therefore requires Node 22.13+ for stable `--permission`.
These restrictions are defense in depth: Node permissions and VM are not an OS
sandbox, and Node 22 permissions do not deny network access. Independent OS-level
effect isolation/observation remains an open P0 acceptance item.

# Benchmark Tasks

Tasks cover a one-line change in a large file, signature plus two callers,
handler validation, a type error, interface-based lookup, React behavior,
three-file edits, structural anti-patterns, external mutation, sequential edits,
monorepo symbol lookup, CRLF, Unicode, and multi-file stale state.

The runnable comparison corpus is `benchmarks/comparison/tasks.ts`: clamped price
calculation, a 2,400-line single edit, signature plus two callers, duplicate-context
selection, coordinated sequential edits, request validation, checkJs type error,
small monorepo lookup, behavior extension, BOM/CRLF/Unicode, mixed endings and
two-module API consistency, and a dirty-worktree task. The price calculation,
large-file and signature tasks form the pilot. The dirty-worktree task stages a
clean baseline, then applies user changes in both the target module and a notes
file before starting either mode. Grading requires those user bytes to survive.

Each task has original files, a golden minimal edit and independent hidden
behavioral checks. Golden diff matching is supplementary: semantically valid
alternative implementations may differ. Preservation checks enforce unchanged
unrelated files and byte fidelity where explicitly requested. The offline suite
also deterministically tests external mutation and stale multi-file preflight;
these are local Patchline safety checks, not model A/B quality measurements.
React and live-model external-mutation scenarios are not implemented in this
initial corpus and must not be inferred from its results.

## Targeted acceptance revision 2 (2026-10-17)

The `targeted` task's editable byte region is the original return statement,
including its indentation and newline. This permits either an inline clamp or
a preceding clamp statement within the function body. The function signature,
braces, leading comment, adjacent `label` function and all other files remain
protected. Behavioral checks still independently verify the clamped result.

Revision 1 permitted only the `percent / 100` expression. That region rejected
a correct preceding clamp statement despite the task prompt allowing it. The
completed `comparison-compact-pilot-2026-10-17` retains its original grading and
corpus fingerprint; it is not regraded with this correction. Future runs use
the changed corpus fingerprint and must not be pooled with revision 1 as if
their acceptance contracts were identical.

# Benchmark Metrics

Record functional success, intended and actual changed lines, unrelated lines,
files touched, formatting churn, whole rewrites, stale overwrites, retries,
context lines, tool bytes, edit bytes, provider token fields when available,
diagnostics latency, route strategy, route confidence, strategy fallbacks,
tool calls saved, and wall time. Search benchmarks should also record files
visited, skipped files, result truncation, and bounded worker concurrency.
Read benchmarks should include file size, requested range, total lines, and
whether a pooled line index was reused. Reports should include warmup count,
measurement count, p50, p95, and p99 latency, plus RSS data where available.
The local runner retains each repeated read's measured duration and returned
`lineIndexReused` flag in `repeatedRead.samples`; its aggregate reuse flag is
derived from those observations rather than assumed from the scenario.
Grep reports should include worker concurrency. Estimated tokens must be labeled
estimates.

The comparison relay records actual provider usage with disjoint input, output,
reasoning, cache-read and cache-write fields. Total is their sum. Missing,
inconsistent or all-zero usage is unavailable, never estimated or called free.
OpenCode step-finish usage is retained separately and deduplicated by part ID;
it is never added again to provider usage. Provider retries count in consumption.
Relay `messageSections` measures each serialized message object's UTF-8 JSON
bytes: system/developer, user/assistant history, tool results, and unknown roles
are disjoint categories. Array brackets/separators are excluded; the complete
messages array size remains in `requestSections.messages`. These are not token
counts. Missing/non-array messages produce `null`, not an invented zero. No
message content is stored in this breakdown.

Comparison `events.toolTiming` separates summed tool duration (`sumMs`), the
union of tool intervals (`activeWallMs`, avoiding overlap double counting), and
the span from the earliest start to latest end (`spanMs`, including gaps).
These are observed timestamp metrics, not a reconstructed dependency critical
path. Nonfinite, negative, reversed or missing timestamps make aggregate timing
unavailable (`null`), with `measured`, `missing` and `complete` retained. Valid
zero-duration intervals remain zero. Error-tool intervals are included.

Success requires behavioral checks, preservation, exit zero and no session error
or timeout. Precision/recall match signed line changes (including position)
against the golden edit. No-op precision is unavailable and recall is zero;
byte-level exactness is recorded separately. All created files are inspected.
Line matching does not imply semantic correctness or style quality.
Preservation also fails when actual deletions include original lines outside the
golden deletion set, even inside a file that was legitimately edited.

Aggregate savings use complete task/repeat pairs and include unsuccessful runs.
If any paired usage is unavailable, aggregate token savings are unavailable.
Cost per successful solution includes expenses of failed attempts. Display median
wall time, per-task values, pass counts, tool errors and raw diffs. At least ten
complete pairs across at least three tasks enable a deterministic 2,000-sample
paired bootstrap, resampling whole task clusters (seed 127019), for 95% savings
intervals. Smaller samples show insufficient data. These intervals condition on
the corpus and do not establish universal model performance. Reports also retain
the subset where both modes succeeded. There is no invented combined quality score.

# Benchmark Reporting

Generated Markdown and HTML evaluate provider tokens, time and outcomes, without
monetary pricing commentary. Token usage remains provider-reported; missing
usage is not estimated from text length.

Streaming response tool-call summaries include content-free fragment counters:
`argumentFragments` counts string-valued argument fragments,
`emptyArgumentFragments` counts its empty-string subset,
`nonStringArgumentFragments` counts present non-string argument values, and
`missingArgumentFragments` counts call deltas without an argument property.
These counters supplement byte counts and hashes without retaining argument
contents. Initialization-only deltas may legitimately omit arguments; a final
zero-byte argument is not proof that a tool received valid empty JSON.

Primary paired analysis includes `quality`: any stock-success/Patchline-failure
pair produces `status: "veto"` with task/repeat identifiers. Otherwise status is
`not-established`, including empty datasets: zero observed regressions do not
establish non-inferiority. Task-ID counts describe grouping, not proven project
independence. Performance improvements cannot override the quality veto.

Attribution execution reserves sequential `attribution-dispatch-NN.json` records
with exclusive creation and fsync before dispatch. An interrupted slot remains
consumed. Reservation rejects skipped or repeated slots; exclusive creation
allows only one winner when multiple callers race for the same slot.
Resume in the same output directory requires an unchanged preparation manifest,
an explicit contiguous ledger, unique completed measurements belonging to
dispatched slots, verified raw artifact bytes/fields, and matching execution
settings fingerprints (model, provider metadata, step limit, and timeout).
Historical reports missing the settings fingerprint cannot be resumed by
inventing a past settings identity. A missing historical
ledger is not reconstructed automatically. The preparation fingerprints the
harness as well as treatment artifacts: changing resume code invalidates an
older preparation. Preserve interrupted evidence rather than rewriting its
manifest. These checks do not constitute authentication against malicious
artifact rewriting or prove end-to-end concurrent runner isolation.

`profile-diagnostic` reports are separate from primary A/B and attribution.
Their JSON and offline HTML include fixed-schedule completeness, duplicate and
unexpected session checks, completed grading, boolean outcomes, and finite
positive token/time totals. Missing usage or nonfinite contrasts withhold savings.
`integrity.complete` means the diagnostic dataset is complete, not that quality
or performance acceptance passed; acceptance remains `not-established-diagnostic`.
The HTML is a descriptive summary; CSV and statistical acceptance are not emitted.

Profile execution reserves each dispatch in an exclusive, fsynced
`profile-dispatch-NN.json` before starting the host. A dispatched attempt consumes
authorization even if no completed measurement survives. Resume uses
`run-profiles --max-sessions 12 --input <out>/results.json --out <out>` with the
original provider/host arguments. It validates the fixed schedule, source/dist/
host/lock identity, contiguous dispatch records and completed result membership.
New profile identities also include a SHA-256 fingerprint of model, steps,
timeout and provider configuration; raw credentials are not written into identity.
Historical executions without this fingerprint fail closed on resume and must
not be upgraded by inventing a historical settings identity.
Resume results must be an array of unique dispatched Patchline-mode entries with completed
grading, boolean success and a measurement-artifact reference containing a local
`attempt-*.json` filename and a SHA-256 digest; the
runner verifies the referenced raw bytes against the digest and checks task,
repeat, profile and mode identity before accepting prior results. Shared raw
measurement fields (including usage and duration) must also match; grading fields
and raw-only process output are excluded from that comparison. This does not
allow removing or replacing raw execution errors: they must remain an unchanged
prefix of the result's errors, with later grading errors allowed to append. This does not
authenticate the grading outcome or establish external provenance.
Resume skips every dispatched entry, including interrupted ones, rather than retrying.
Legacy ledgers must be explicitly reconstructed from evidence and labelled as
such; a missing ledger is rejected. This does not replenish authorization.
Artifact identity is checked before dispatch and after raw measurement persistence,
before grading; changed artifacts stop the run without deleting raw evidence.

`run-attribution` requires `--input <manifest.json>`, `--max-sessions 18`,
`--provider-config`, and all four artifact paths used for preparation. It executes
the manifest's fixed three-treatment order with fresh workspaces and homes, pins
model/steps/timeout to preparation, and revalidates preparation before and after
each session. Raw measurements are persisted before grading and partial reports
survive a later failure. Attribution reports remain separate from primary A/B
analysis; a pilot cannot establish acceptance. Usage accounting uses tokens.

Provider SSE tool-call telemetry stores argument byte counts and SHA-256 hashes,
JSON validity, and read-path/anchor-offset validity flags, never argument contents.
Reassembly is bounded to 2 MB of stream text and 128 calls. Malformed, interrupted,
or budget-exhausted streams are marked incomplete; non-SSE responses have no
tool-call telemetry. These diagnostics do not reconstruct historical payloads.

Reports contain raw JSON plus a concise Markdown summary. Precision ratios are
supplementary; they do not replace correctness, stale safety, or raw counts.

The A/B runner adds an autonomous Russian `index.html` with responsive charts,
token composition, filters, hidden-check results and expandable source diffs.
`results.json` is the authoritative portable artifact; `results.csv` and
`summary.md` are supplementary. The browser report makes no network requests.
Embedded JSON escapes HTML delimiters and model/file output renders as inert text.
Unknown usage and tariffs remain explicitly unknown. Pilot status, experiment
limits, mode order, version digests and methodological caveats are visible.
Statistical summaries reject non-finite or negative durations and token counts
before pairing, confidence intervals, or projections. Missing tokens remain
`null`; invalid numeric values are not silently filtered or converted to zero.
Manifest completeness also requires a finite, nonnegative duration for every
session; failures appear in `integrity.invalidDurations`. Projection labels use
the declared `fullProjection.sessions`, never a hard-coded corpus size.
Markdown interpretation follows the declared stage: full-series results retain
task/model/condition limitations and uncertainty guidance instead of being
mislabelled as a pilot. Incomplete-series warnings remain independent of stage.
The comparison runner accepts `--repeats 1..5` (pilot default 1). Live full-stage
runs require exactly 5 repetitions; fewer repetitions are rejected before sessions
launch and must use the pilot stage.
The declared manifest and `--max-sessions` cap are checked before paid sessions;
increasing repeats does not bypass the session cap.

## Three-treatment attribution preparation

The `report --input <results.json>` command recognizes `attribution-pilot`
separately and emits authoritative JSON, a descriptive Markdown summary, and
CSV rows keyed by task/treatment/repeat, plus an offline HTML summary with
escaped analysis text. Missing token usage is an empty CSV cell, not zero.
This route does not use the primary two-mode HTML renderer.

`verify-attribution --input <attribution-manifest.json>` with the same four
binary/plugin flags as preparation revalidates the fixed design and fingerprints
without reading provider configuration, launching hosts, or authorizing sessions.

The separate attribution design uses `stock`, `original`, and `optimized`
treatment identities. Do not collapse the latter two into the two-mode runner's
`patchline` identity or feed these runs to its paired completeness analysis.
The proposed pilot has three tasks (`targeted`, `large-file`, `three-files`),
two repetitions, and 18 sessions. Task and treatment orders reverse on repeat 2.

Preparation manifests have `executionAuthorized: false`; creating one does not
authorize provider requests. They pin model, temperature, limits, corpus hash,
the schedule, canonical artifact paths, byte counts, entry SHA-256 hashes and
plugin-directory tree fingerprints. Both plugin treatments share one integrated
host. The manifest also pins the complete comparison-harness tree (including
runner, grader and reporting sources); verification rejects missing or changed
harness fingerprints, so older preparation artifacts must be prepared again.
The current repository source tree and root `package-lock.json` bytes are also
pinned and revalidated. These identify preparation inputs; they do not prove
source-to-dist correspondence or fingerprint installed dependency contents.
Distinct plugin paths with identical entry bytes are rejected.
Snapshots are rechecked before exclusive manifest creation; existing files are
never overwritten. Manifest output must be outside both measured distributions.
It must also be outside measured dependency installations, preventing manifest
creation from contaminating its own dependency snapshot.
The schedule dispatcher revalidates the preparation manifest immediately before
and after each awaited callback. An artifact mutation stops dispatch before the
next session; callbacks run serially in the fixed schedule.
Each callback receives its schedule identity and a detached copy of the matching
verified treatment artifact, including canonical binary/plugin paths and profile.
This binds future process selection to the verified treatment rather than a
separate caller-maintained mode mapping.
The helper does not grant execution authorization or implement provider execution
by itself.
On success it returns all callback results in schedule order, including failed
session results and unknown usage. A result is appended only after its post-run
manifest verification succeeds; dispatch errors propagate to the caller.
An optional awaited checkpoint receives a copied, readonly cumulative result
array after each verified result, allowing partial-series persistence before a
later session fails. Checkpoint errors stop subsequent dispatch as well.
An optional abort signal is checked before verification, before dispatch and
after checkpointing. Cancellation prevents later sessions; an already running
callback remains responsible for its own process cancellation and cleanup.
Each plugin additionally fingerprints the complete sibling installation
`../node_modules` tree, including a canonical path, when present; absence is
recorded as null and later appearance invalidates preparation. This captures
that installation's bytes, not proof of the host's conditional module resolution
or dependencies resolved from other ancestor directories.

Attribution completeness requires exactly the declared 18 identities, complete
grading, positive finite token totals and positive finite durations. Attribution
summary completeness additionally requires a boolean success outcome for every
session; invalid outcomes are listed in `integrity.invalidOutcomes` and suppress
all savings contrasts. Only literal `true` counts as successful.
Descriptive totals include failed-session costs. Savings are withheld for incomplete series;
the three descriptive contrasts are `originalVsStock`, `optimizedVsOriginal`,
and `optimizedVsStock`, each using its own baseline denominator for tokens
and duration. Original-versus-stock does not use optimized-treatment costs.
Even complete pilot summaries say `not-established-pilot` and cannot establish
quality non-inferiority or performance acceptance. Provider cache is uncontrolled.
The preparation helpers are not yet an executable three-treatment experiment;
host dependency-resolution evidence and approved execution limits remain
prerequisites for connecting provider execution; the dispatcher supplies the
manifest revalidation boundary.

The runner exposes a preparation-only command: `prepare-attribution --stock-bin
<stock> --patchline-bin <integrated> --original-plugin <baseline-dist/plugin.js>
--optimized-plugin <current-dist/plugin.js> --out <existing-or-new-output-dir>`.
It creates `attribution-manifest.json` exclusively and does not load provider
credentials or dispatch model requests. Model/limits in this preparation design
are fixed by the manifest helper; execution remains unauthorized.
Preparation rejects explicit model, steps, timeout, session-cap, repeats, variant,
tool-profile and stage overrides instead of silently ignoring them.
Conversely, original/optimized plugin flags are rejected by the primary runner,
which cannot select those artifacts; preparation and verification accept them.
`verifyAttributionManifest` rechecks the fixed preparation design, corpus,
schedule and current host/plugin/distribution fingerprints. It rejects stale or
altered preparation data and does not convert preparation into execution approval.

# Configuration

Plugin options are passed through the OpenCode plugin tuple:

```json
{
  "plugin": [["opencode-patchline", {
    "mode": "precision",
    "maxInitialReadLines": 120,
    "maxSearchResults": 30,
    "maxDiagnostics": 30,
    "applyPatchFallback": true,
    "hashlineRecovery": false,
    "telemetry": false,
    "summary": true
  }]]
}
```

Options may set read/search/diagnostic limits, snapshot TTL, generated-file
patterns, explicit full-replacement allowlists, local summary output, and
validation commands. `hashlineRecovery` defaults to `false`; when enabled, only
upstream-proven ordinary Hashline anchor recovery is allowed. `REM` and `MV`
remain strict stale-safe operations. Invalid options fail during plugin load.

`maxInitialReadLines` sets the default file-read range and the hard directory
entry bound. Explicit file `read.limit` values may request up to 2,000 lines;
output remains bounded and continuation observes only displayed lines.

`precision` (the default) overrides the editing tools and guards direct shell
writes. `compatibility` leaves the built-in `read`, `edit`, `write`, and
`apply_patch` tools and shell behavior untouched while retaining Patchline's
additional discovery and diagnostic tools. The snapshot-dependent
`patchline_edit_batch` tool is available only in `precision` mode. `disabled`
registers no tools.

`applyPatchFallback: false` rejects classic `apply_patch` fallback sections.
Use `patchline_apply_patch` for snapshot-tagged Hashline sections. Native
OpenCode `apply_patch` remains available for large or unsupported operations and
invalidates affected Patchline snapshots.
`maxDiagnostics` bounds diagnostic output to that many lines, in addition to
the hard 20,000-character safety cap. `telemetry: false` does not retain
detailed local events; aggregate counters remain available to the optional
`patchline_summary` tool. Setting `summary: false` omits that tool entirely.

## Project LSP

`lspAutoSetup` and `lspAutoInstall` default to `true`. The former controls project
language/server preparation during plugin startup; the latter permits managed
server installation where a recipe supports it. Set `lspAutoInstall: false` for
discovery without automatic package installation, or `lspAutoSetup: false` to
disable automatic preparation. `lspMaxEntries` bounds discovery (default 30,000);
`lspStorageDirectory` overrides the dedicated managed-server cache.

These runtime options are separate from installer `--no-lsp`, which skips only
installer-side TypeScript provisioning/settings. OpenCode's `lsp: false` and
custom/disabled server entries are honored. Use `lsp check`, explicit `lsp setup`
and `patchline_lsp_status` as described in [doctor](doctor.md).

Installer state is runtime ownership metadata and should not be committed to
source control. Project-local state is ignored by the repository policy. A
failed local install restores the captured package manifest and lockfiles when
npm changed them without an external intervening edit. The shell-write guard
is best-effort detection; OpenCode permission checks remain the authoritative
enforcement boundary.

For mixed line-ending files, unchanged prefix and suffix bytes are preserved.
Newline characters in the changed region use the dominant line ending from
the original document, while BOM and final-newline shape are preserved.

# Doctor

`opencode-patchline doctor` checks Node.js, OpenCode, plugin SDK, Hashline,
ast-grep, filesystem round trips, stale rejection prerequisites, CRLF, BOM,
native LSP flags, and a TypeScript LSP setup check. On Node.js, the Bun-native
upstream Hashline adapter is an optional capability; exact snapshot edits remain
available. The check distinguishes the Node fallback from the full Bun/native
Hashline runtime. It does not modify OpenCode configuration.

For a release archive, invoke the adjacent CLI with Node.js:

```bash
node /path/to/package/dist/cli.js doctor
node /path/to/package/dist/cli.js doctor --lsp --directory /work/project --json
node /path/to/package/dist/cli.js lsp check --directory /work/project --json
node /path/to/package/dist/cli.js lsp setup --directory /work/project
```

`doctor --lsp` and `lsp check` inspect language roots and server availability
without installing packages. They report preparation, not a verified connection.
`lsp setup` explicitly prepares managed servers where supported. OpenCode-managed
servers and installed toolchains remain in use; disabled/custom configuration is
preserved. Managed npm servers use pinned recipes and a dedicated cache rather
than editing the project's package manifest or installing globally.

`patchline_lsp_status` shows project preparation and connection state in the agent
session, with a conversation card in the integrated TUI. `patchline_lsp` performs
queries and connection checks. Prepared, installed or configured does not prove
a successful handshake. Missing toolchains must be installed using their normal
language-specific installation method.

Managed storage is `%LOCALAPPDATA%/opencode-patchline/lsp` on Windows and
`$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode-patchline/lsp` (default `~/.local/share/...`) elsewhere.
It is independent of installer-owned TypeScript/Bun dependencies and retained
on plugin removal. Restart OpenCode after changing plugin/configuration options.

# Installation

Patchline 1.4.0 is distributed as a GitHub release archive, not an npm registry
publication. See the complete [English](../../README.md#installation) and
[Russian](../../README.ru.md#установка) installation instructions. Configuration
is loaded at startup; fully restart OpenCode after updates.

Run `node /path/to/package/dist/cli.js doctor` after installation. This release targets
OpenCode 1.18.x–1.19.x.

## Installer

```bash
node dist/cli.js install --local --lang en
node dist/cli.js install --local --global --lang ru
node dist/cli.js host-upgrade --opencode-version 1.19.0
```

Requires Node.js >=20 and OpenCode >=1.18.0 <2. Package registration delegates to
`opencode plugin`, which installs package dependencies and registers the server
and TUI exports. Project configuration is discovered at the Git root (or current
directory outside Git), including `.opencode/`. Global configuration follows
OpenCode's XDG directory, overridden by `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR`.

Run the local command from the newly extracted package to update an existing
registration. Keep the package directory in place while it is registered.
For a source checkout, run from the project to configure:

```bash
npm install
npm run build
node dist/cli.js install --local --lang ru
node dist/cli.js uninstall --dry-run --lang ru
```

Both POSIX and PowerShell wrappers use their adjacent built package from a release
or checkout, without npm CLI fetching. Missing builds give setup instructions.
They preserve caller cwd, literal arguments and exit codes. Install defaults to
the adjacent source; an explicit `--package` replaces it. For example:

```bash
sh /opt/patchline/package/install.sh --project --cwd /work/project --lang en
sh /opt/patchline/package/install.sh --global --yes
sh /opt/patchline/package/install.sh --project --cwd /work/project --dry-run
```

```powershell
& "C:\tools\patchline\package\install.ps1" --project --cwd "C:\work\project" --lang ru
& "C:\tools\patchline\package\install.ps1" --global --yes
```

Add `--global` for global scope, `--project` for explicit project scope,
`--cwd <path>` to select a project, or `--yes` to accept installer prompts.
`--dry-run` previews without changes, locks, commands, downloads or builds.
`--no-host` skips the shared UI host; `--no-lsp` skips LSP provisioning/settings.
Bun provisioning is independent. `--host-binary <path>` explicitly selects the
executable when preparing the host. Use `install --help` for the full flag list.
Values accept separate or equals-style arguments; duplicate/conflicting options
are rejected. `--local` selects the package source, not project scope.
Native host targets cover Windows/Linux/macOS x64/arm64; manager/platform smoke
coverage is documented in the installer contract.

The installer checks the supported add-ons independently. If
`typescript-language-server` is missing, it asks before running `npm install
--save-dev` (project) or `npm install --global` for missing `typescript` and
`typescript-language-server` packages. If `bun` is missing, it separately asks
before installing the global `bun` package for the full native Hashline runtime.
Existing direct package dependencies are not claimed or removed. Without an
interactive terminal, each dependency installation is skipped unless `--yes` is
supplied. User-disabled or custom TypeScript LSP configuration is preserved.

`--lang en|ru` / `--language en|ru` localizes only installer and uninstaller
messages. Language and dependency ownership are stored in
`.opencode-patchline-state.json` in the project root or global configuration
directory. Package-manager and OpenCode subprocess output uses their own language.

### Installing a checkout

```bash
npm install
npm run build
node dist/cli.js install --local --lang ru
```

`--local` registers the package containing the running CLI instead of the npm
registry version. Run it from the project that should receive the plugin, or
include `--global`.

## Uninstaller

```bash
node dist/cli.js uninstall --dry-run
node dist/cli.js uninstall --lang ru
node dist/cli.js uninstall --global --yes
```

`--dry-run` lists changes without writes or package-manager commands. Normal
removal asks for confirmation; `--yes` accepts it. Use the same scope as installation.
The uninstaller removes Patchline strings/tuples from both server and TUI JSON or
JSONC configurations and removes unchanged installer-owned TypeScript LSP settings.
Only the recorded, allowlisted LSP packages are passed to npm uninstall. Other
plugins, user settings and previously present dependencies remain intact.

Configuration edits preserve comments, BOM and line endings. All files are
preflighted before mutation; symlinks, invalid UTF-8/JSONC and stale files are
rejected. Writes are atomic, with unique `.patchline-backup-<id>` copies retained.
A configuration transaction rolls back already-written files on failure unless a
concurrent change prevents safe rollback. Dependency-removal failure retains the
state so a retry can finish cleanup. Successful removal deletes installer state.
OpenCode's shared plugin cache is retained, as it may be used by another scope.

`--keep-deps` retains dependencies and runtime add-ons. Regular removal leaves
the integrated host and releases its recorded owner after successful cleanup.
`--restore-host` restores the verified original executable/version only when no
other recorded owners remain, and reverts only an unchanged owned autoupdate
preference. Legacy rotating backups are not eligible. Delayed restore can use
`--host-binary <path>`. See [uninstallation](uninstallation.md) for recovery.

Restart OpenCode after either operation.

# Troubleshooting

`STALE_SNAPSHOT` requires a fresh narrow read. `WRITE_PROTECTED` requires
anchored edit. `PATH_OUTSIDE_WORKSPACE` indicates traversal or symlink escape.
`CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE` means the optional provider is disabled; editing
safety remains active. Restart OpenCode after plugin or config changes.

## Installation and removal

- Missing adjacent package/build: extract the complete release archive and run
  `npm install --omit=dev`, or run `npm install` and `npm run build` in a checkout.
  A standalone wrapper does not download a CLI from npm.
- Wrong project: pass `--project --cwd <path>`; the Git root is selected from that
  directory. `--local` chooses a package source, not the scope. Use `--global` for
  global configuration.
- Host/package mismatch after updating to 1.4.0: rerun the new package's installer
  in the affected scope, restart OpenCode and run its doctor. `host-upgrade`
  expects a matching integrated host/package and does not update Patchline.
- No verified original backup: an old integrated host cannot be assumed stock.
  Remove Patchline registrations, then reinstall OpenCode using its original
  install method. `.patchline-previous` may contain another integrated build.
- Other host owners: remove their registrations with the matching project/global
  scope before requesting `--restore-host`. Missing state files do not prove
  ownership was released; do not delete recovery records to bypass the guard.
- Changed binary/backup/state or interrupted lock: inspect the reported path,
  retain recovery files, and retry after resolving the actual conflict.

Use `--dry-run` to inspect planned actions and `--keep-deps` to preserve package
dependencies. [Removal](uninstallation.md) explains delayed host restoration.

# Uninstallation

```bash
node dist/cli.js uninstall --dry-run
node dist/cli.js uninstall --lang ru
node dist/cli.js uninstall --global --yes
node dist/cli.js uninstall --project --cwd /work/project --keep-deps --yes
node dist/cli.js uninstall --global --restore-host --dry-run
node dist/cli.js uninstall --global --restore-host --yes
```

Run from the extracted release package and use the same scope as installation.
Normal removal asks for confirmation;
`--dry-run` previews without writes or package-manager commands, and `--yes`
accepts the confirmation for automation.
Use `--cwd <path>` to select the project, `--project` for explicit project scope,
and `--help` to see command-specific flags. Values also accept `--flag=value`.

Patchline registrations are removed from server and TUI JSON/JSONC configuration.
Direct `opencode-patchline` dependencies in the selected project/config root and
project `.opencode/package.json` are uninstalled with npm (lifecycle scripts
disabled). Other dependencies remain. Package cleanup is included in dry-run.
The equivalent wrappers are `sh uninstall.sh` and `./uninstall.ps1`; arguments
are forwarded, and project scope follows the caller's working directory.
Unchanged installer-owned LSP settings, recorded LSP packages and runtime add-ons
are removed. Only installer-owned `bun` is removed globally; existing Bun
installations remain. Other plugins and previously present dependencies are
preserved. Unique
`.patchline-backup-<id>` files remain beside changed configurations. Successful
removal deletes installer state. The shared OpenCode package cache is retained.

Restart OpenCode after removal. See [installation](installation.md) for scope,
language, ownership and recovery details.

## Dependencies and original host

`--keep-deps` retains direct Patchline dependencies, recorded LSP packages and Bun,
while still removing registrations and unchanged owned LSP settings. Regular
removal retains the integrated host and releases its recorded owner only after
package cleanup succeeds. Failed cleanup retains state for retry.

`--restore-host` restores the verified `<binary>.patchline-original`, using the
ownership and SHA-256 record in `<binary>.patchline-recovery.json`. It refuses
restoration if any other recorded project/global owner remains, or if the binary,
backup or ownership record changed. Original backups are immutable across host
upgrades; restoring returns the saved original version, not the latest upstream.
Legacy installations without a verified original are not inferred from rotating
`.patchline-previous` files; use your original OpenCode install method to repair
those manually after removing Patchline registrations.

Only an unchanged installer-owned `autoupdate: "notify"` preference is reverted.
Other user settings, comments and formatting remain. The host, backup, receipt
and affected settings are rechecked under lock after confirmation. Backups and
recovery evidence remain after restoration. Delayed restore after normal removal
is supported; add `--host-binary <path>` if OpenCode is no longer discoverable.
Unrecorded/manual plugin installations cannot be enumerated automatically.
Keep the package directory while the shared integrated host still uses its CLI.

# Upgrade Policy

Before supporting a new OpenCode minor version, rerun capability probes and
verify plugin load, duplicate tool ordering, before-hook cancellation, tool
schemas, session/worktree context, and LSP gating. Safety behavior is never
silently downgraded.

## Independent versions

For the 1.4.0 GitHub archive, download the archive and SHA256SUMS.txt, verify the
checksum, extract to a new permanent directory and install runtime dependencies.
Run the new adjacent installer in every affected scope:

```bash
sh /path/to/patchline-1.4.0/package/install.sh --project --cwd /work/project --lang en
sh /path/to/patchline-1.4.0/package/install.sh --global --yes --lang en
```

PowerShell uses the same flags with `install.ps1`. Restart OpenCode and run the
new package's doctor. Keep the old package until no scope references it. Upgrading
from a legacy integrated host does not create a verified stock-original backup.

- `install --local` updates Patchline on the installed OpenCode upstream version.
- `opencode upgrade` and the OpenCode 1.19 TUI update service invoke the same
  host-only operation. They pass the running binary path and full expected version.
- `node dist/cli.js host-upgrade --opencode-version 1.19.0` changes only OpenCode.
  It never registers the plugin or changes its dependency or configuration files.
- `--host-binary <path>` selects a specific installation; unknown/ambiguous
  launchers are rejected. `--rebuild` repairs the same version after adapter changes.
- Host updates require matching host/package versions, a per-binary exclusive
  lock, source ownership validation, frozen upstream dependencies, version probes
  before/after installation, and guarded binary rollback.

OpenCode 2 migration is rejected for an integrated host until a compatible
Patchline version is installed. External manager updates (npm, Homebrew, Scoop,
Chocolatey, etc.) cannot be intercepted by an inactive plugin. After such an
update, rerun the existing package's local installer to rebuild on the newly
installed upstream version. Keep the release directory in place: the host's
upgrade entrypoint is anchored to that package, not to npm's `latest` tag.

Windows can retain a running old image after replacement. Locked, integration-owned
retired backups are retained; no unrelated process is terminated. An interrupted
update's `.patchline-update-lock` must be inspected before removal/retry.

Verified original backups survive managed host upgrades. `uninstall
--restore-host` returns the saved original version, even if an integrated host
was upgraded later, and refuses restoration while another recorded owner remains.

## Everyday workflow

1. Locate the target using `patchline_lsp` for symbols, `patchline_grep` for literal
   text, or `ast_search` for syntax structure.
2. Read the smallest useful range with `read`. The response includes the file
   path, snapshot ID, Hashline tag and observed line anchors.
3. Edit only observed content using the returned snapshot. Do not invent tags,
   snapshot IDs or anchors.
4. Inspect the result and diff, then run project diagnostics or tests.

Explicit reads support up to 2,000 lines. Bounded responses expose a continuation
offset; only displayed lines are available as edit anchors.

## Exact edits

Call `edit` with values from the latest `read`:

```json
{
  "filePath": "src/example.ts",
  "snapshot": "<snapshot returned by read>",
  "oldString": "<observed text>",
  "newString": "<replacement text>"
}
```

`newString: ""` deletes the observed text. Use `write` only for new files.

## Hashline and batches

Use `patchline_apply_patch` for Hashline sections. Replace the tag and line
number below with values actually displayed by `read`:

```text
[src/example.ts#<tag returned by read>]
PUT 12.=12:
+replacement line
```

`patchline_edit_batch` preflights multiple snapshot-linked edits before writing.
`patchline_execute` selects an exact, Hashline, batch or standard-tool route.
Inspect each result before the next call. See the [Hashline contract](../specs/hashline-contract.md).

## Native patches and recovery

OpenCode's native `apply_patch` remains available for large files, large changes
and operations outside Patchline's capabilities. Read changed files again after
a native patch before using snapshot-based tools.

- `STALE_SNAPSHOT`: read the current file and rebuild the edit from observed text.
- `fallback_required`: use the `nextTool` reported in the response.
- `WRITE_PROTECTED`: use snapshot-linked `edit` for an existing file.
- Permission denial: request the required OpenCode permission. External absolute
  read/edit paths require `external_directory` and operation-specific permission.
- Failed native context match: read the affected range and rebuild the patch.

Never use shell writes to bypass a rejected edit. Preserve user changes and
unrelated formatting. See [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

## Validation

Use `patchline_diagnostics` for a configured diagnostic command, native LSP when
available, and the project's normal typecheck/tests. Commands require OpenCode's
permission for the exact operation. Use `patchline_summary` for local counters.
For environment checks, run `node dist/cli.js doctor` from the extracted package.

# Работа с Patchline

[English](usage.md) · [Руководство](../../README.ru.md) · [Установка](../../README.ru.md#установка) · [Конфигурация](configuration.md) · [Контракты инструментов](../specs/tool-contracts.md)

## Обычный рабочий процесс

1. Найдите нужный код: `patchline_lsp` для символов, `patchline_grep` для текста,
   `ast_search` для синтаксических структур.
2. Прочитайте минимальный полезный диапазон через `read`. Ответ содержит путь,
   snapshot, Hashline-тег и якоря прочитанных строк.
3. Измените только прочитанный код, используя полученный snapshot. Не придумывайте
   теги, идентификаторы snapshot и якоря.
4. Проверьте результат и diff, затем запустите диагностику или тесты проекта.

Явный диапазон чтения поддерживает до 2 000 строк. Ограниченный ответ сообщает
следующий offset; для якорей доступны только действительно показанные строки.

## Точные правки

Вызовите `edit` со значениями из последнего `read`:

```json
{
  "filePath": "src/example.ts",
  "snapshot": "<snapshot returned by read>",
  "oldString": "<observed text>",
  "newString": "<replacement text>"
}
```

`newString: ""` удаляет прочитанный текст. `write` используется только для новых файлов.

## Hashline и многофайловые правки

Используйте `patchline_apply_patch` для Hashline-секций. Замените тег и номер
строки значениями, которые действительно показал `read`:

```text
[src/example.ts#<tag returned by read>]
PUT 12.=12:
+replacement line
```

`patchline_edit_batch` предварительно проверяет несколько snapshot-правок до записи.
`patchline_execute` выбирает точную правку, Hashline, batch или стандартный инструмент.
Проверяйте каждый ответ перед следующим вызовом. Подробнее: [контракт Hashline](../specs/hashline-contract.md).

## Обычный apply_patch и восстановление

Обычный `apply_patch` OpenCode доступен для больших файлов, больших изменений и
операций вне возможностей Patchline. После него заново прочитайте изменённые
файлы перед использованием snapshot-инструментов.

- `STALE_SNAPSHOT`: заново прочитайте файл и пересоберите правку по текущему тексту.
- `fallback_required`: используйте `nextTool`, указанный в ответе.
- `WRITE_PROTECTED`: существующий файл меняется через snapshot-правку `edit`.
- Отказ в разрешении: запросите нужное разрешение OpenCode. Для внешних абсолютных
  путей нужны `external_directory` и разрешение соответствующей операции.
- Ошибка совпадения контекста обычного patch: прочитайте диапазон и пересоберите patch.

Не обходите отказ записи через shell. Сохраняйте пользовательские изменения и
несвязанное форматирование. Подробнее: [решение проблем](troubleshooting.md).

## Проверка результата

Используйте `patchline_diagnostics` для настроенной команды диагностики, нативный
LSP при наличии и обычные проверки типов/тесты проекта. Команды требуют разрешения
OpenCode на конкретную операцию. `patchline_summary` показывает локальные счётчики.
Для проверки окружения выполните `node dist/cli.js doctor` из распакованного пакета.

# Editing Rules

1. Existing source files require snapshot-anchored edit.
2. Verify the live file immediately before writing.
3. Reject stale state with zero writes.
4. Make the smallest semantically correct change.
5. Preserve unrelated code, formatting, imports, comments, BOM, and endings.
6. Never replace current user changes with Git HEAD.
7. Never turn a patch failure into an unrequested whole-file overwrite.
8. Track and justify every fallback.

# Generated File Rules

- Change generator inputs, not generated outputs.
- Update lockfiles through the package manager.
- Do not patch build, distribution, coverage, vendor, or minified output.
- Permit exceptions only through narrow explicit configuration.

# Model-Facing Policy

```text
PATCHLINE EDITING POLICY
- When the exact path is known, read that file directly using the smallest useful range; skip discovery searches.
- Locate only when the path or target is unknown; use available LSP for symbols, grep for text, and AST for structure.
- Read the smallest useful source range; use read with anchor and limit for a known unique literal target, without offset. Resolve ambiguous candidates before editing.
- Use snapshot-anchored Patchline edits for precise local changes.
- Select by change scope, representation, and supported operations, not file size alone. Use ordinary apply_patch beyond Patchline limits or for unsupported operations.
- Hashline sections belong to patchline_apply_patch, not ordinary apply_patch.
- Re-read files after ordinary patches before further Patchline edits.
- Never rewrite an existing source file for a local modification.
- Preserve unrelated code and formatting exactly.
- If a snapshot is stale, reread before retrying.
- Run relevant diagnostics and proportional validation after edits.
```

The compact policy includes a generic anchor-read example:
`read({"filePath":"src/main.ts","anchor":"function main","limit":40})`.
For a known file and unique literal target this replaces grep followed by read;
omit `offset` and resolve ambiguity before editing. The example is guidance,
not evidence of reduced model calls or tokens.

When OpenCode configuration explicitly sets `lsp: false`, Patchline omits
`patchline_lsp` and `patchline_lsp_status` from its registered tool map. The
configuration hook applies this before tool registry enumeration in OpenCode
1.19.0. In the extended profile, re-enabling LSP on a subsequent configuration
callback restores the definitions; an already cached host registry still
requires OpenCode restart.
Previously captured tool definitions also reject execution while `lsp: false`
is active, before permission prompts, discovery, or SDK/CLI requests.
Absence of `lsp: false` is not proof of a working language server. After its
configuration callback, the compact profile offers LSP only when project
preparation returned a verified document/workspace-symbol capability. Disabled
automatic preparation, missing/unverified servers, unsupported symbol
capabilities, or preparation failure omit the tool. Each configuration callback
clears the previous reports before preparing again. The compact operation enum
contains only verified `documentSymbol`/`workspaceSymbol` operations; it does
not advertise LSP diagnostics because initialization alone does not verify the
host diagnostic bridge. Previously captured definitions enforce the current
operation capabilities before path discovery, permissions, or requests.
This confirms server initialization capability, not end-to-end host bridge
success for every project. Toolchain-change invalidation remains a separate
gate.
Compact LSP definitions are removed while preparation is pending. Results from
an older configuration callback cannot replace reports or restore definitions
after a newer callback has started (including explicit LSP disablement).

Plugin option `toolProfile` accepts `extended` (default, previous tool surface)
or `compact` (opt-in). Compact precision exposes `read`, `edit`, `write`,
`patchline_edit_batch`, `patchline_grep`, `ast_search`, `patchline_diagnostics`
and `patchline_lsp` (eight plugin tools, seven with explicit `lsp: false`).
Host-native tools are additional; these counts do not describe the full request.
The compact profile omits adaptive/Hashline routers, search routing, standalone
LSP status and activity summary. Its policy directs exact edits to `edit` and
related edits to `patchline_edit_batch`, retaining native patch fallback.
All mutation guards and validation are shared with the extended profile.
Compact uses a dedicated policy rather than filtering the extended Hashline
instructions. Its regression budget is below 1800 UTF-8 bytes (the previous
filtered policy was 2168 bytes). It retains direct-path discovery avoidance,
bounded anchor reading, selector exclusion, latest observed snapshots, stale
recovery, unrelated-code preservation and native-patch mismatch recovery.
It also requires relevant diagnostics and proportional validation after edits.
This byte budget measures policy text only; it is not a provider-token budget
or evidence of fewer model turns. Extended policy remains separately defined.
Compatibility mode still uses host-native read/edit/write; it does not gain
precision tools by selecting compact. Switch back to `extended` to restore the
previous definitions. Configuration changes require an OpenCode restart.
Compact is not yet the default: schema-byte measurements, host integration and
live quality/cost comparisons must establish the final profile first.

# Patchline Policy

Locate precisely. Read minimally. Patch exactly. Verify immediately.

The current working tree is authoritative. User changes have priority over Git
HEAD, caches, previous snapshots, and model assumptions. Safety enforcement
belongs in tools; model instructions express strategy only.

Keep ordinary OpenCode apply_patch available for large files, large changes,
and unsupported precision operations. Hashline uses patchline_apply_patch.
External absolute targets require OpenCode directory and operation permissions.

# Search Routing Rules

- Use LSP for symbols and relationships.
- Use grep for literal text and configuration keys.
- Use AST search for syntax structure.
- Use direct read when the target path and range are known.
- Stop after a conclusive result.
- Bound results and context; do not search for confidence theater.

# Security Rules

- Keep edits inside the canonical worktree.
- Reject `.git`, traversal, malformed paths, and symlink escape.
- Preserve OpenCode permissions.
- Use raw content digests, never timestamps alone, for stale checks.
- Reject invalid UTF-8 rather than corrupting bytes.
- Do not send source or metrics remotely by default.

# Validation Rules

- Run cheap relevant checks after a source edit.
- Report validation failures separately from edit failures.
- Prefer changed-file and targeted package checks.
- Expand validation with task risk.
- Inspect the final diff when Git is available.
- Never claim success without fresh verification output.

# Skill Usage Policy

Use TDD for behavior changes, architecture review before widening interfaces,
and fresh verification before completion claims. Skills do not override
