# Anchored Edit Contract

Status: Accepted

Existing source files require a snapshot obtained from `read`. Exact edits must
match a unique `oldString` within observed lines unless explicitly replacing
all observed matches. Hashline patches must carry the same observed tag and
pass Hashline preflight. Candidate content is constructed before any write.

Snapshot IDs are exact-content identifiers. Four-character Hashline tags are
display anchors only: if a tag maps to more than one recorded content version,
Patchline rejects the edit instead of selecting a candidate. Live content must
also retain the recorded raw digest and file identity through commit.

Exact replacement text is literal. A terminal newline belongs to its source line,
not a nonexistent next line. Exact and proven linear Hashline operations transfer
observed-line provenance according to actual edits. Whole Hashline headers may
use the full snapshot ID to resolve a short-tag collision safely.

# AST Search Contract

Status: Accepted

Cancellation is checked before native parsing and during traversal. Traversal
rejects beyond 100,000 visited or pending nodes. Native synchronous parse itself
cannot be interrupted by an event-loop callback.

AST search is reserved for syntactic structure. It uses `@ast-grep/napi`,
loads language support on demand, caps results, and reports parser failures.
Literal text belongs to grep; symbol relationships belong to LSP.

Source input is limited to 8 MiB before UTF-8 decoding or native parsing,
including growth detected while the opened file is read. Oversized input is
rejected with `INVALID_ARGUMENT`. Each returned node preview is capped at 2,000
characters while retaining its file and line range.

Result limits are integers from 1 through 500. AST traversal stops after one
match beyond the requested limit, returns at most the requested number of
matches, and sets `truncated` when an additional match exists. The service does
not materialize an unbounded match-result array.

# Compatibility Specification

Status: Accepted

Patchline targets OpenCode `1.18.x`–`1.19.x`, Node.js 20 or newer, and the public v1
plugin API. Capability detection is mandatory: unavailable native LSP or AST
bindings disable only the affected feature. A changed plugin tool ordering,
missing execution hook, or unavailable session/worktree identity is a hard
compatibility failure for precision mode.

The 1.4.0 release baseline is OpenCode `1.19.0`; its integrated host version is
`1.19.0+patchline.1.4.0`. Current dependencies are `@opencode-ai/plugin@1.19.0` and
`@oh-my-pi/hashline@18.1.5`. Hashline is loaded lazily because its published
runtime targets Bun. Node installations retain exact edits and linear PUT/CUT
Hashline edits through the guarded fallback; structural blocks, registers, and
file operations remain capability-gated and report through doctor.

The integrated conversation host preserves native `apply_patch`, `edit`, and
`write` availability for every model. Its installer recognizes the pinned
upstream model-selection branches, applies an idempotent replacement, and
rejects unknown source shapes before installing a new binary. Stock hosts may
still filter native `apply_patch` by model; restart/rebuild the integrated host
after this migration to enable the fallback for non-GPT models.
The integrated version derives from upstream and package versions without a
private revision suffix. `smoke:host`
copies the installed executable into an isolated PATH and builds/installs there;
the default lifecycle smoke checks registration and removal via command injection.

Tool availability and Patchline policy are provider-neutral: GLM, DeepSeek,
MiniMax, Qwen, Kimi and future tool-capable models receive the same guarded
editing contract. The system hook inserts its exact policy at most once and
includes concrete JSON/exact/Hashline guidance without changing host prompts.
The host smoke verifies native and Patchline tool object schemas for 17
provider/model identifiers spanning direct providers, OpenRouter and OmniRoute.
These are offline registry checks, not provider connectivity or model quality
claims; remote inference and provider-side schema acceptance require configured
credentials and separate API runs. Provider reasoning/schema transformations
remain owned by OpenCode; Patchline does not disable them or weaken guards.

# Deep review hardening

## Implemented contracts

- Every path resolution with an authorization callback authorizes the canonical
  target. The OpenCode adapter uses worktree-relative operation permission
  patterns internally and requests external-directory permission externally.
- Generated-file protection applies at common edit preflight, not only write or
  whole-patch entry points.
- Exact replacement text is literal, including dollar sequences. Candidate CRLF
  text is normalized before diff analysis. Final newline anchors do not require
  a nonexistent next line. Exact operations map observation provenance from the
  actual replacement rather than an ambiguous line diff.
- Mixed-newline reconstruction preserves unchanged line chunks; changed chunks
  use the dominant ending. Its matching budget is 100 ms / 2,000 edits.
- Hashline tag normalization scans each line linearly. Full Patchline snapshot
  IDs may be used in whole-patch headers to resolve short-tag collisions; the
  upstream runtime receives the corresponding short tag after scoped lookup.
- Pure additions/deletions use direct statistics. Node insertion anchors require
  complete decimal tokens and safe integer values.
- Oversized snapshots fail explicitly instead of returning an already-evicted
  ID. Budget-only failure after an edit preserves the applied change and reports
  no next snapshot plus a warning. Unexpected bookkeeping failures still invoke
  guarded rollback; callers must inspect landed/restored/conflict details.
- Mutation reads are bounded to 8 MiB. Prepared edit batches have a 32 MiB
  accounting budget. Hashline live reads are sequential and check cancellation.
- Recovery results are bound to the baseline used for calculation; warning text
  is not a safety proof. Changed baselines reject before commit.
- Existing-file edits serialize commit/rollback across overlapping canonical
  paths process-wide. Atomic replacement rechecks an expected content digest
  after temporary preparation. External writes in the final check/rename window
  remain outside a portable compare-and-swap guarantee.
- Move rollback invalidates source and destination snapshots.
- Registration failure invokes the host rollback callback; project preflight
  runs before host provisioning. Already-installed host configuration changes
  also return a rollback callback. Both host caches validate their upstream tag.
- Doctor timeout attempts Windows process-tree termination. SDK LSP rejects error
  envelopes and forwards cancellation; its output is bounded. AST checks
  cancellation before parsing and during traversal. Native synchronous parsing
  cannot be interrupted by an event-loop abort callback.
- Literal search scans lines by offsets instead of allocating a split array and
  uses normalized line numbering, including bare CR.
- Hashline live input is limited to 4 MiB aggregate before upstream preparation.
  Clipboard limits are 256 registers / 8 MiB per scope, 512 scopes, one-hour idle
  expiry and a 64 MiB global accounting eviction budget checked on scope access.
- Linear Hashline operations preserve observation provenance in Node and, where
  the independently calculated result matches upstream, Bun. Full-ID repeated
  sections with conflicting identities reject before parsing.
- Allowed existing-file replacement writes share canonical path locks with edits.
  Queued lock acquisition supports cancellation without allowing later callers
  to overtake an active holder.
- Host binary verification failure attempts ownership-checked restoration. All
  four host source adapters preflight before the patch set is committed; build
  failures restore owned source changes. Installer version checks share doctor's
  stable-version policy.
- SDK LSP has a 15-second deadline. AST traversal has a 100,000-node visited/pending
  budget. Search enumerates at most 100,000 files / 10,000 directories and sorts
  files once. These are hard refusal budgets, not partial-result truncation.
- Windows process-tree cleanup has its own two-second fallback deadline. Host
  source inspection rejects tracked modifications outside the four adapter files
  and Bun lockfiles; allowed adapter modifications still require deeper ownership
  inspection. Host smoke separates plugin tools from the native host apply_patch.

# Diagnostics Contract

Batch, classic-create, adaptive exact and Hashline mutation results include failed post-edit validation
reasons in model-facing text as well as metadata. The reason precedes per-file
summaries so summary truncation does not hide the validation failure.
Failed post-edit command summaries identify the command and either its exit code
or timeout. Empty stdout/stderr is explicitly reported as `(no output)` rather
than producing an empty failure reason.

Status: Accepted

Diagnostics are proportional to risk and bounded. Patchline distinguishes tool
execution success from validation success. Native OpenCode diagnostics are
preferred; configured commands provide a deterministic fallback. A diagnostics
failure does not conceal a successful write and is reported separately.

Configured commands run only after OpenCode grants `bash` permission. Captured
stdout and stderr are bounded while the process runs, and the final combined
output, including its truncation marker, never exceeds 20,000 characters.
Timeout expiry marks validation unsuccessful, terminates the command process
tree, closes inherited output pipes, and settles without waiting indefinitely
for descendants.
Results expose `timedOut` separately from `ok` and `exitCode`. Timeout output
includes the configured deadline even when captured logs are truncated, within
the same 20,000-character budget. The model-facing diagnostics tool labels a
timeout as incomplete validation, rather than a clean check or a normal exit
failure with an unknown code. Post-mutation validation retains the timeout
reason alongside the applied-write status.
OpenCode tool cancellation is propagated to the command runner and uses the
same process-tree cleanup before rejecting with the abort reason.

# Encoding Preservation

Status: Accepted

Exact input line separators normalize to LF before matching and analysis.
Candidate bytes must decode to the analyzed normalized text. Literal replacement
does not expand JavaScript dollar patterns. Mixed-ending files preserve unchanged
line chunks between separate edits; new/changed chunks use the preferred ending.

Patchline supports UTF-8 with or without BOM and preserves LF or CRLF. Invalid
UTF-8 is rejected instead of decoded with replacement characters by read, edit,
literal grep, and AST search. Mixed line endings are preserved for unchanged
text by exact editing; Hashline batch edits use the file's detected dominant
shape and are reported by doctor/tests.

# Generated File Specification

Status: Accepted

Known build output, vendored content, minified bundles, generated clients, and
lockfiles are protected. Patchline recommends the canonical generator or
package manager. Generated detection is conservative and configurable. The
same protection applies to new-file batches: a batch is rejected during
preflight if any requested target is a known generated path, and no file is
created.

The common edit preflight enforces this protection for exact edits, exact batches,
single-file Hashline and whole-patch Hashline, including move destinations.

# Hashline Contract

Status: Accepted

`patchline_apply_patch` uses the current `@oh-my-pi/hashline` section format for
existing files. Ordinary OpenCode `apply_patch` retains its classic patch format:

```text
[path/to/file.ts#TAG]
PUT 12.=12:
+replacement line
```

`TAG` is the four-hex content fingerprint shown by `read`. The full Patchline
snapshot ID is also accepted by the `edit` tool. A short tag is resolved only
when it identifies exactly one recorded content version; tag collisions fail
closed and require the full snapshot ID or a fresh read.

All edits are strict by default. Patchline checks session, worktree, canonical
path, snapshot digest, file identity, and parent identity before writing. When
`hashlineRecovery` is enabled, ordinary Hashline edits may use upstream recovery
against live normalized content, but only when every anchored line maps
unambiguously; changed or ambiguous anchors still fail closed. `REM` and `MV`
never use recovery.

The Bun runtime applies the upstream whole-patch semantics, including line
ranges, insertions, structural blocks (`N*`), anonymous and named clipboard
registers, same-path section merging, and file operations (`REM`, `MV`). Named
registers persist only within the session/worktree clipboard scope and failed
batches do not publish tentative register state. Hashline mutations in one
session/worktree are serialized so concurrent calls observe and publish clipboard
state in order. Node retains the bounded linear
`PUT`/`CUT` fallback and rejects unsupported structural, clipboard, and file
operations rather than applying them heuristically. If live content drifted,
the Node fallback rejects with `STALE_SNAPSHOT`; it never writes the old
snapshot over external changes. OpenCode's Bun process is the full runtime.

Every multi-operation patch is parsed and preflighted in memory before the
guarded commit. Overlapping ranges, unseen lines, malformed headers, mismatched
paths, and mismatched tags produce a zero-write error. `REM` and `MV` use guarded
rename/link operations with parent, identity, digest, destination, and rollback
checks; a later failure reports landed writes and preserved conflicts.

The snapshot store indexes exact IDs and tag candidates independently. Multiple
reads of byte-identical content merge their displayed line provenance; distinct
contents remain separate even when their short tags collide.

# Installer and uninstaller contract

Status: Accepted

Both commands support `--project` (default), `--global` / `-g`, `--cwd <path>`,
`--lang en|ru` / `--language en|ru`, `--yes` / `-y`, `--help` / `-h`,
`--dry-run`, and `--host-binary <path>`. Install additionally supports `--local`,
`--package <built-directory>`, `--no-host`, `--no-lsp`, and `--opencode-version`.
Uninstall additionally supports `--keep-deps` and `--restore-host`.
Values accept separate or equals-style arguments. Unknown, repeated, missing,
boolean-valued switches and conflicting flags fail before filesystem changes.
`--project` conflicts with `--global`; `--local` conflicts with `--package`.
`--no-host` conflicts with explicit host/version selection. `--local --global`
remains valid: local selects the adjacent package source, not the scope.
Help returns without filesystem inspection or subprocesses. Dry-run validates
selected configuration/package inputs and reports paths/actions without writes,
locks, prompts, subprocesses, downloads or builds. Explicit directories contain
a Patchline manifest and built CLI/server/TUI, and supply host adapters/version.
`--no-lsp` skips LSP provisioning/settings independently of Bun. `--no-host`
skips provisioning and records ownership if an existing tracked host is used.
`--keep-deps` retains direct dependencies and recorded LSP/runtime packages;
registration and unchanged installer-owned LSP settings are still removed.
Uninstallation checks its initial state snapshot before mutation and completion.

not the npm registry's latest version. An explicit `--opencode-version` remains an

cannot upgrade another installed version. CLI and TUI share `Installation.upgrade`.
Unknown install methods are allowed only for integrated hosts, whose update does
not invoke the original package manager. Unsupported major migrations fail safely.

Native targets are selected for Windows/Linux/macOS x64/arm64. Native executables,
canonical symlinks, official npm launchers/cached binaries and npm Windows shims
are discovered. Unknown or ambiguous launchers require an explicit binary path.
Per-binary locks serialize installation/update. Source caches are per package and
upstream version so different released packages do not rewrite each other's adapters.
All owned legacy adapters are recognized by exact reconstruction, not marker alone.
Retired Windows backups locked by running processes are retained after verification.
External manager updates require integration repair; an inactive plugin cannot
intercept them. Native artifact selection does not imply every manager is CI-tested.

Installation delegates server/TUI registration and plugin dependency resolution

The installer checks each add-on independently, installs only missing packages,

Installer language preferences affect installer/uninstaller messages only.

Failed local dependency installation captures package manifests and lockfiles
after the npm command returns (including partial failures). Rollback verifies

Later external edits are preserved and reported as conflicts. External edits
during the npm subprocess itself cannot be attributed reliably; this remains a
best-effort process boundary rather than an atomic filesystem transaction.
Installer state is checked against the last installer-owned snapshot and restored
byte for byte. Independent rollback stages continue after a conflict and rollback
is attempted only once. A new configuration containing unrelated settings is
edited to remove owned registration rather than deleted.
Failed dependency cleanup retains the current ownership state for recovery and
reports the non-zero cleanup exit code instead of declaring rollback successful.

Repeated installation uses `opencode plugin --force` when the selected scope

are preflighted and checked again before npm; failure retains installer state for

Root `install.sh`, `uninstall.sh`, `install.ps1` and `uninstall.ps1` require Node.js
>=20 and invoke the adjacent built `dist/cli.js` from a release or checkout.
They validate `package.json`, forward literal arguments and preserve the exit
code/caller's working directory. Install defaults to `--local` unless an explicit
source was supplied. Missing package/build gives release/build instructions
without registry lookup; `src/` is not required. POSIX wrappers convert Node paths
using `cygpath` where available (Git Bash).

Unless `--no-host` is supplied, installation provisions a host from the installed
stable upstream version, or explicit `--opencode-version <1.x.y>`. Patchline

`<upstream>+patchline.<plugin>` (for example `1.18.34+patchline.1.1.0`). Exact
matching installed pairs skip rebuilding. Upstream and plugin changes therefore
update their respective components independently. Invalid versions fail closed.
It installs Bun when missing, prepares a matching tagged checkout, adds tool
replacement slots and a coordinated update adapter, and builds without embedded
web UI. Unsupported upstream source APIs fail before replacing the executable.
Replacement requires confirmation unless `--yes` is supplied. One fixed
`.patchline-previous` backup is rotated; byte-identical installs do not rotate it.
Command `opencode` is retained. Unsupported platforms fail instead of claiming
full UI installation. Regular removal retains the shared host; `--restore-host`
restores a verified original under the same per-binary lock.
Legacy UUID backups and source caches are retained until ownership-aware cleanup
is implemented; they must not be deleted merely by matching a filename.

After registration, all recognized historical Patchline package/local paths are
collapsed to one selected package entry per config, preserving tuple options.
Similarly named third-party packages are retained. Before provisioning (including
the already-installed fast path), the installer changes global `autoupdate` from
missing/true to `"notify"`, preserving false/notify and unrelated JSONC content,
with guarded writes and backups. This prevents OpenCode's startup updater from
replacing the custom version with stock. Integrated `opencode upgrade` delegates
to the same local installer with the requested upstream version. Startup update
comparison ignores integration build metadata to avoid repeated same-version

the installer, global transaction journaling and managed cleanup remain pending.
The preference is retained on regular uninstall. Existing global configuration is
required for provisioning. Executable discovery canonicalizes the located path
(including NVM aliases) before regular-file, parent and identity checks.

The scope-specific state records the registered package specifier, language and
allowlisted installer-owned additions. Missing state never authorizes arbitrary
package removal. Uninstallation requires confirmation unless `--yes` is supplied.
Dry-run must not write files, create backups, run npm or delete installer state.

Configuration discovery is bounded to the selected project/Git worktree or global

encoding markers and line endings. All candidate files are preflighted before
mutation. Unsafe paths, symlinks, malformed configuration, unsupported encoding,

Multi-file failures roll back applied configuration writes only while their
post-write contents/identities still match; conflicts retain backups and report
failure. Dependency-removal failures retain state for retry.

Successful removal deletes state, retains other plugins and the shared OpenCode
package cache, and reminds the user to restart OpenCode.

## Original host recovery

Before the first stock replacement, `<binary>.patchline-original` is created
exclusively and never rotated. `<binary>.patchline-recovery.json` records its
SHA-256, original stable version, installed SHA-256, absolute state-file owners
and the original autoupdate value when changed. Repeated installs and host-only
upgrades preserve the original. Provisioning claims its owner while holding the
host lock; ordinary removal releases it only after package cleanup succeeds.
Installed Bun is recorded for normal cleanup, and newly provisioned Bun is
removed after failed host preparation; pre-existing Bun is not claimed.
Rollback restores recovery metadata only after a successful binary rollback,
with snapshot/identity guards. Original copies and recovery receipts are retained.

`--restore-host` preflights owner conflicts before uninstallation writes. Other
recorded owners block restoration even if their state files are missing; missing
state is not evidence of release. Unknown/manual installations are not enumerable.
Legacy integrated binaries without a verified original cannot be restored using
rotating backups. Current binary and original hashes/identities, receipt and any
owned config changes are checked again under lock after confirmation. Restore
returns the saved original version, not the latest upstream. Only a still-notify
owned autoupdate setting is reverted; other user changes remain. Global plugin
removal and preference restoration in the same file are combined into one edit.
Delayed restore after regular removal works with a discoverable or explicitly
selected binary. Restoration rolls back guarded writes on failure, preserving
recovery evidence and reporting conflicts instead of overwriting external edits.

`npm run smoke:installer-flags` exercises project/global wrapper installation,
preview and removal in an isolated environment. `npm run smoke:host-restoration
-- <stock-opencode-binary>` exercises real native file replacement and restoration
through the uninstaller without building a new host or changing the current one.

# LSP Contract

Status: Accepted

An empty SDK workspace-symbol response is returned as `data: []` with a
`capabilityNote`: it does not prove that the project has no symbols. Some hosts
expose a placeholder HTTP endpoint even while native LSP works. Use native LSP,
AST search or literal search to verify. Nonempty SDK responses retain their
existing representation; this note does not claim that every empty result is
a capability failure.

Runtime LSP dispatch checks the JSON configuration content associated with cached
reports as well as its generation. An in-place configuration edit clears reports,
advances the generation and removes compact LSP exposure before dispatch. A fresh
configuration setup or successful explicit status refresh establishes a new
content baseline. Verified command reports also retain executable/launcher identity
fingerprints (canonical paths, file identity, size and nanosecond timestamps),
command arguments, working directory, PATH and NODE_OPTIONS. Project-root and
ancestor-directory package
manifests and dependency lock metadata (npm, pnpm, Yarn, Bun, Cargo, Go, uv and
Poetry) are additional invalidation inputs, checked up to the filesystem root.
This does not cover arbitrary edits inside installed dependencies. Bare executable names are
resolved through PATH rather than treated as workspace files. Dispatch rechecks
these identities before and after asynchronous host operations, revoking compact
exposure when they change. This is not a transitive dependency-content fingerprint:
a dependency edit that leaves launcher and lock metadata unchanged remains a
separate gate.
Initial configuration publication and explicit refresh recheck configuration
content after asynchronous fingerprinting; neither publishes stale capabilities
when the configuration object is edited in place during that wait.
Runtime fingerprint checks recheck cancellation and generation before revocation;
an obsolete in-flight check cannot clear capabilities published by a newer setup.
Explicit status refresh also snapshots configuration content before preparation
and rejects if it changes in place, rather than treating discarded reports as a
successful empty discovery or establishing a baseline from an obsolete refresh.

Preparation health probes terminate their process tree before returning either
verified capabilities or an error. A successful initialize response does not
leave a background language server running; runtime requests use the host's
managed server instead.
Cancellation of preparation propagates to the caller. Existing, newly installed
and rustup-managed server probe failures must not convert an aborted request into
a configured-but-unverified report or continue installing another server.
Preparation rechecks cancellation after asynchronous executable/runtime discovery,
rustup execution and managed installation before starting the next operation.
Configuration publication rechecks cancellation, original `lsp` identity and its
JSON configuration content after preparation. Replacing, editing in place or
disabling that value while preparation is pending
discards the old reports and does not overwrite the newer configuration.
Preparation also compares JSON configuration content after discovery/runtime/
installer boundaries before starting the next operation. A changed configuration
returns no reports and does not start another install or probe; already running
work retains its existing timeout/cancellation behavior.
The initialize request uses the actual project directory URI for both `rootUri`
and `workspaceFolders`, rather than a placeholder workspace. Capabilities from a
probe remain scoped to the project root that was initialized.
Probe JSON-RPC framing counts raw UTF-8 bytes, retaining incomplete frames across
stdout chunks. Unicode notifications before initialize responses cannot shift
the next frame or turn healthy capabilities into a parsing failure.
Health probes limit headers to 8 KiB and total stdout to 1 MiB; unsafe or larger
declared body lengths fail before waiting for the body. Error details retain only
the last 4,000 characters. These limits apply to preparation probes, not normal
host LSP sessions.
Initialize results require a non-null, non-array capabilities object. Missing or
malformed capabilities fail verification; an empty object is valid but grants no
provider operations.

SDK symbols responses are inspected for error envelopes. Requests forward abort
signals and share one 120-second default deadline across status and symbol
requests; output is bounded to 200,000 characters. Symbol results require a direct
array or an SDK envelope with an array-valued `data` field; null, missing data,
objects and stringified arrays are unavailable rather than successful responses.
When the SDK exposes LSP status,
workspace search requires at least one connected client in the requested
directory. Empty/disconnected status is capability-unavailable; status errors or
malformed responses are unavailable, never a successful empty search. A connected
client's genuine empty symbol result remains valid. Older clients without the
status method retain the existing request path. The status SDK signature does
not accept a signal; the wrapper bounds its wait but cannot cancel that underlying
request. Symbol requests receive the combined cancellation signal.
An SDK method's presence and a server initialize capability are not proof that
the host HTTP operation is implemented. In the inspected integrated host
1.19.0+patchline.1.4.0, the `/find/symbol` handler returns an unconditional empty
array. Empty results cannot distinguish this stub from a legitimate no-match
response. Workspace-symbol integration remains unverified for that host; a
successful direct language-server request does not close the host integration gate.
File-specific plugin calls authorize the canonical target before CLI execution.
The CLI bridge itself rejects explicit `lsp: false` before executable discovery,
file resolution, or process creation, including calls outside the plugin hook.
The plugin config hook also returns before project preparation when `lsp: false`,
after clearing capability reports and removing LSP tools. Explicitly disabled
LSP therefore does not traverse the worktree or probe/install servers during
plugin configuration. Re-enabling configuration still follows normal preparation
and capability verification; a stale in-flight preparation cannot republish tools.
An explicit `patchline_lsp_status` call rechecks discovery and server health with
installation disabled, rather than returning startup reports indefinitely. For
the canonical plugin worktree it clears cached capabilities before preparation
and publishes only the latest configuration/refresh generation. Failed or aborted
refreshes leave no verified cached capability. Status for another worktree cannot
replace the plugin worktree's reports. This explicit refresh is not automatic
toolchain fingerprint invalidation; that gate remains open.
If configuration changes or a newer same-root refresh supersedes a pending status
request, the pending request rejects with `CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE` instead of
returning an obsolete verified report to the model.
In compact mode, a final `CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE` from the runtime bridge revokes
cached capabilities and removes the LSP tool for the canonical plugin worktree.
A captured tool handle then fails its capability guard without another host call.
Only the current generation can be revoked; other worktrees cannot clear it.
Configuration reload or explicit status refresh can verify capabilities again.
Runtime operations capture their configuration generation before path resolution
and permission. They recheck cancellation/generation before SDK/CLI dispatch,
before fallback and before returning output; a changed generation rejects with
`CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE` rather than dispatching or publishing obsolete results.
In the compact profile, document-symbol execution additionally requires the
canonical file to be inside an existing, canonical project root whose preparation
report verified `documentSymbolProvider`. A verified sibling project does not
authorize the request; missing or inaccessible roots fail closed before bridge
execution. This initialization evidence does not prove document indexing or
end-to-end host availability.

The fallback order is the active OpenCode SDK symbol client, native OpenCode
LSP, the CLI bridge, AST, then grep. Workspace-symbol requests use the active
SDK client when available, avoiding an isolated process; document symbols and
diagnostics retain the CLI bridge. OpenCode 1.18.30 exposes model-facing LSP
only when `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_LSP_TOOL` or global experimental mode is enabled.
Patchline does not start a duplicate server for OpenCode-native recipes. Its
optional CLI bridge is exposed as `patchline_lsp` rather than `lsp`, preserving
OpenCode's native experimental tool when that capability is enabled.

Patchline discovers supported language projects recursively, excluding repository
 dependencies, generated directories, hidden control directories, and
 symlinked directories. Discovery uses extensions, manifests, nearest project
 roots, and shebangs, and may return multiple servers for a monorepo.

The registry covers OpenCode's common native servers and managed npm recipes for
servers not provided by the current OpenCode installation. Explicit `lsp: false`,
per-server disabled entries, and custom commands remain authoritative. Managed
installations live outside the project in a per-user cache, use exact package
versions, an inter-process lock, temporary directories, a completion marker, and
no lifecycle scripts. Project toolchains remain requirements rather than being
silently installed by scanning.

Within one preparation call, projects sharing a managed npm server share its
installation result, including failures. A failed download is not retried for
each project root. The next preparation call retries, so installing or repairing
the toolchain does not leave a persistent negative capability cache. Successful
commands still require a separate initialization handshake for each project root;
installation reuse never grants another root verified capabilities.

Preparation reports distinguish `configured`/`native` from `verified`. A server
is verified only after a bounded LSP `initialize` handshake; finding an executable
on PATH alone is not a working connection. Failed optional setup is reported by
`patchline_lsp_status` and does not prevent OpenCode startup.

Automatic setup is controlled by `lspAutoSetup`, `lspAutoInstall`, `lspMaxEntries`,
and `lspStorageDirectory`. CLI `lsp check` performs discovery without
installation; `lsp setup` permits managed installation. Both support
`--directory` and `--json`.

When the native tool flag is disabled, Patchline's `lsp` tool bridges
`workspaceSymbol`, `documentSymbol`, and diagnostics through the installed
OpenCode CLI. Definition/reference/call hierarchy remain native-only.

The CLI bridge never invokes a shell. It propagates OpenCode tool cancellation,
has a 120-second execution deadline to allow slow OpenCode LSP startup, and bounds each captured output stream to
200,000 characters so an unhealthy CLI cannot retain unbounded memory. A
successful explicit empty JSON result (`[]` or `{}`) is accepted for diagnostics.
Empty or whitespace-only diagnostics stdout is `DIAGNOSTICS_UNAVAILABLE`, with
`validation: "unverified"`; exit code zero alone does not prove clean validation.
Empty symbol results
are returned as `CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE` with an explicit native-LSP/AST/grep
fallback hint, since the isolated CLI request cannot prove that a document or
workspace index has been initialized. Disabled or unconfigured LSP is reported
with the same capability error rather than being misreported as no symbols. The bridge requests OpenCode startup logs at INFO level to make
that distinction observable without changing the user's OpenCode configuration.
Capability errors include the requested `operation`. Disabled/unconfigured LSP
adds `lsp: "disabled"`; empty symbol output adds `indexing: "unverified"`. These
are distinct degraded states and integration checks accept the host's actual
state rather than requiring indexing to be unverified when LSP is disabled.

# Multi-File Edit Contract

Status: Accepted

All paths, snapshots, operations, and candidate bytes are validated before the
first commit. Duplicate targets are rejected using canonical, platform-aware
path identity. Originals are retained until the
batch completes. A commit error triggers best-effort restoration and reports
both landed and restored files. Rollback compares the current bytes with the
Patchline bytes before restoring; if an external change landed after a commit,
Patchline preserves it and reports the path as a rollback conflict.

Edit-batch rollback also retains the identity of each file after its commit and
requires both that identity and the committed bytes to match before restoring
the original. A same-byte replacement is preserved and reported as a conflict.

Create batches use the same guard. Before removing a partially created file,
Patchline re-resolves its canonical identity and compares its current bytes
with the bytes written by Patchline. External replacement, symlink swaps, and
content changes are preserved and reported in `details.conflicts`.

Create-batch rollback also retains the created file identity and requires both
identity and digest to match before removing a partially created file. A
same-byte replacement is therefore preserved as an external conflict.

Creation bookkeeping obtains those bytes and identity from the exclusive `wx`
file handle before path-based rollback checks, so a replacement immediately
after creation cannot be mistaken for the Patchline-created file. Bytes are
read positionally from offset zero on that handle after writing, ensuring an
unchanged partial creation is recognized and removed during rollback.

Existing-file commits and rollback restores write a temporary file in the target
directory and atomically replace the target entry. This prevents a target
symlink swapped after the final identity check from redirecting Patchline bytes:
the operation rejects the swap and never follows it. New-file creation remains
exclusive and never replaces an entry that appeared after preflight.

Atomic replacement retains the parent directory identity from preflight and
checks it before temporary-file creation and before the final rename. A parent
directory replacement therefore rejects the write instead of redirecting it.

New-file creation re-resolves the target after recursive parent creation and
before the exclusive `wx` open. A parent-directory symlink or canonical target
change detected in that interval is rejected; the same guard applies to single
`write` creation and create batches.

File snapshots created by `read` also retain the platform file identity. Edit
commit rejects a target that was replaced by another file even when its bytes
still match the snapshot. The snapshot recorded after a successful edit tracks
the new identity obtained from the temporary file before atomic replacement.
It does not infer that identity from the target path after commit, so a
same-byte replacement in that interval cannot receive a trusted next snapshot
or be mistaken for the Patchline-written file during batch rollback.

# Native patch context recovery

## Ownership and classification

Native `apply_patch` remains a host tool. Patchline's renderer presents its errors
without executing, retrying or weakening host verification. On an error result,
the phrases `Failed to find expected lines` / `context does not match` identify a
presentation-only `NATIVE_PATCH_CONTEXT_MISMATCH`. Generic verification failures
are not enough: malformed syntax and permission failures remain distinct.

The renderer shows `Patch rejected · context mismatch`, one concise reason, a
single fresh-read recovery action and expandable native details capped at 2,000
characters. Mutation route reasons
are separate from failure reasons. Patch-header paths are presentation hints, not
permission evidence. Native write counts remain unknown unless supplied by trusted
metadata; no `writes: 0` is inferred from message text.

## Recovery

Read the smallest affected range and rebuild the patch using exact current lines,
including line breaks. Never repeat the unchanged failed patch, reconstruct old
content from a summary, or overwrite a file to bypass rejection. A small unique
replacement can use snapshot-aware exact editing after the read. Successful native
patches require a new read before reusing Patchline snapshots.

## Evidence and remaining integration work

The inspected OpenCode v1.18.34 `src/tool/apply_patch.ts` derives update content for
each hunk inside the preflight loop (including matching failures), then asks edit
permission and enters the file-change write loop. That source-level evidence shows
context matching preceding writes in this version; it does not prove transactional
rollback for I/O failures or the entire supported version range.

Unit regression scenarios cover single-file errors, CRLF multi-file headers,
trusted and absent write metadata, unrelated errors, malformed patch envelopes,
successful states and route/failure separation. The mounted TUI smoke checks the
actual error card and fresh-read guidance.

The installed plugin SDK exposes `event`, and its event union includes
`message.part.updated` with tool part error state. Patchline now observes these
events to count native context mismatches, deduplicated by session/call ID in a
1,000-entry bounded set. It retains neither patch text nor error source context.
The counter is available as `nativePatchContextMismatches` in the local summary.
Counts only reflect events actually received; they do not infer retries or success.
Events without a valid session/call identity are ignored so malformed host payloads
cannot inflate the counter. Deduplication is bounded and cleared on plugin dispose.

- Controlled-provider host session smoke now passes locally through the real
  `/session/:id/message` loop: native multi-file mismatch performs no writes,
  fresh read and recovery patch succeed, and the plugin summary records exactly
  one mismatch without retaining source text. The smoke does not claim autonomous
  LLM retry behavior; that still requires a model-backed session.

A direct run of the v1.18.34 upstream `test/tool/apply_patch.test.ts` was attempted
in an existing isolated host checkout. It failed before running tests because the
checkout lacked host dependencies; the clean-checkout CI job subsequently passed
the exact suite on Windows, Linux and macOS.

# Observability Contract

Status: Accepted

Local events track mechanism, paths, observed lines, bytes, snapshots, edit
ranges, diff counts, stale conflicts, retries, durations, diagnostics, guarded
writes, and fallbacks. Remote telemetry is off and not implemented by default.
Metrics never include source content.

## Explicit comparison artifacts

The opt-in `benchmark:compare` runner is separate from plugin telemetry. It writes
fixture source diffs, model/tool results, checks and actual provider usage to a
user-selected local directory. It never embeds provider credentials or forwards
events to a telemetry service. It supports only bounded, explicitly requested
live runs and does not treat absent usage or unconfigured model pricing as zero
cost. Its HTML report must render embedded source as inert text. Its input
fixtures are disposable; existing worktree state and runtime guards are preserved.

# Path Security Contract

Status: Accepted

Paths are resolved from the tool context worktree and canonicalized. Service
calls remain worktree-bound unless supplied an explicit authorization callback.
The OpenCode adapter permits explicit absolute external paths only after
`external_directory` and operation-specific read/edit authorization against
the canonical target. Relative traversal and workspace symlink escapes remain
rejected, as do lexical and canonical `.git` internals.
External snapshots remain scoped to the originating session and worktree;
the worktree is never expanded to a drive or common ancestor. Commit and
rollback repeat path authorization and existing identity/digest checks.

Authorization callbacks also receive canonical internal targets. Operation
permission patterns are worktree-relative internally; path aliases cannot change
the authorized resource. LSP file requests follow the same canonical checks.

Parent creation traverses relative components from the caller's workspace root;
it never computes a traversal between canonical and lexical path spellings.
Caller root aliases are supported, while each nested target is still checked
against the canonical workspace and protected Git paths.

# Performance and compatibility budgets

- Literal search returns actual absolute file paths, including subdirectory and
  authorized external-directory searches. Results retain deterministic path order.
- Search scans ordered batches of at most eight files and stops consuming batches
  after one match beyond `maxResults`. Each file retains at most `maxResults + 1`
  matches. Skipped counts describe the consumed prefix, not the entire workspace.
  Enumeration and sorting still cover the selected tree. Cancellation is checked
  before traversal, during enumeration, between batches and during line scanning;
  an in-flight bounded file read may complete before cancellation is observed.
- Mutation diff analysis uses a 100 ms diff-algorithm deadline and a 2,000-edit
  limit. Exceeding either rejects preflight with `STANDARD_TOOL_REQUIRED`, before
  writes. These limits do not weaken stale or observed-line checks. Tokenization
  and line mapping remain bounded by the existing file size limit.
- Snapshot byte accounting includes pooled source buffers/text, an estimate of
  eight bytes per line-index entry and 32 bytes per observed-line set entry.
  The quota is an accounting estimate, not a hard process-RSS limit. Shared
  documents/indexes are charged once; observed sets are charged per snapshot.
  A prepared read carries its digest into recording without hashing twice.
- Host version generation and doctor accept stable OpenCode `>=1.18.0 <2`, with
  integration build metadata accepted by doctor. This range is a compatibility
  policy, not proof that every upstream version has been integration-tested.
  UI patching validates all replacement anchors before writing the renderer.
- Doctor version probes have a 10-second deadline and a 16,384-character combined
  output cap. Exceeding either terminates the probe and reports it unavailable.
- CLI installer code is imported only after a valid install/uninstall request
  passes argument parsing (help does not initialize it), or after host-upgrade
  arguments pass validation. Capability inspection is loaded when an inspection
  command needs it, preserving injected inspection hooks. This defers startup
  work; it neither removes installation guards nor skips doctor self-tests.
- CLI LSP project preparation is imported only within the LSP command branch,
  after validating `--directory`. Configuration and explanatory commands do not
  initialize LSP discovery; LSP command behavior and verification remain intact.
- AST search loads the native parser only after argument, path, language and
  bounded UTF-8 file checks pass. Plugin/module import and rejected requests do
  not load the native binding. Cancellation is checked before and after loading;
  the first valid AST request pays initialization, later requests reuse the module.

Further implemented budgets and limitations are specified in
`deep-review-hardening.md`: linear tag normalization, 32 MiB prepared edit data,
4 MiB aggregate live Hashline data, clipboard quotas, search/AST traversal caps,
SDK deadline and bounded process cleanup. RSS remains an estimate rather than a
hard allocation ceiling. Hidden-whitespace measurements are reproducible with
`npx tsx benchmarks/hardening.ts`.

# Snapshot Contract

Status: Accepted

A snapshot records the canonical path, normalized content, raw SHA-256 digest,
Hashline tag, observed line set, text shape, session ID, workspace/worktree
identity, and creation time. A snapshot must not be used by another session or
worktree. Expired and least-recently-used entries are removed without changing
files. The store also applies a bounded byte quota with content pooling for
byte-identical documents. Pooled documents retain a normalized line index for
range rendering without materializing a full line-string array on every read;
the index is derived from the same snapshot content and does not change stale
validation. Scope-specific observed lines remain independent.

Byte accounting includes line indexes and observed sets. Same-content rereads
merge observations only when the file identity remains the same. A snapshot that
cannot fit its own quota rejects before an ID is published. Budget-only failure
after a committed edit/move yields an applied result with no next snapshot and a
warning. Tag whitespace normalization is linear in source length.

# Stale Edit Contract

Status: Accepted

Immediately before preflight, Patchline reads current raw bytes and compares
their SHA-256 digest with the snapshot. A mismatch returns `STALE_SNAPSHOT`,
sets `rereadRequired` to true, and performs zero writes. There is no force
overwrite default. Recovery is allowed only when the current target bytes are
unchanged.

# Tool Contracts

Status: Accepted

`patchline_lsp_status` reports per-project preparation and verified connection
state. Its conversation renderer is registered alongside every other server
tool; prepared/configured/installed is not a verified LSP connection.

In precision mode, hosts exposing `jsonSchema` in `tool.definition` receive an
additional provider-facing `not: { required: ["anchor", "offset"] }` constraint.
Runtime selector rejection remains authoritative; older hosts without that
schema hook retain runtime validation. This does not guarantee model compliance.

`read` accepts `filePath`, `offset`, `anchor`, and `limit`. Optional `anchor` is
validated after a required nonempty string `filePath`; invalid paths are rejected
with `INVALID_ARGUMENT` before permission callbacks or path handling. The anchor is
nonempty literal text matched against the LF-normalized file, not a regex. It
must occur exactly once (including overlapping occurrences); the returned page
starts at the line containing that occurrence. Missing/ambiguous anchors,
directory anchors, and combining `anchor` with `offset` are `INVALID_ARGUMENT`.
Selector validation errors explicitly instruct callers to retry with `filePath`
and one selector, omitting the other property entirely; `limit` may be retained.
Rejected selector combinations create no snapshot and authorize no edit.
Both tool profiles publish separate offset/anchor call examples and explicitly
require omitting unused selector properties, rather than supplying defaults or
empty placeholders. This guidance does not relax argument validation.
Missing/ambiguous match errors include up to eight candidate line numbers and
`details.truncated`; repeated occurrences on one line remain distinct matches.
Only nine occurrences are inspected to determine truncation. Candidate hints
do not create a snapshot or mark any source lines as observed.
Existing size/output limits and observed-range snapshot guards apply equally
to anchored reads. Supplied `offset` and `limit`
values must be positive integers; invalid direct service calls are rejected
instead of silently clamped. `maxInitialReadLines` controls the default file page
and directory page cap. Explicit file limits may request up to 2,000 lines.
File reads return a snapshot tag and numbered source lines. Directory reads
return sorted entries without a snapshot; empty directories accept offset 1.
Empty files report zero source lines. File pages are bounded to 20,000 characters
and include only complete source lines. Responses expose `requestedLimit`,
`truncated`, and `nextOffset`; only rendered lines become observed anchors.
`edit` accepts `filePath`, `snapshot`, and either
exact strings or a Hashline patch in the extended profile. In compact precision,
only exact-string arguments are exposed; supplying `hashlinePatch` directly is
`INVALID_ARGUMENT` before permissions or filesystem activity. Extended exact
and Hashline semantics are unchanged.

The exact-string form uses `oldString`/`newString`. `write` accepts `filePath` and
`content`, creating only new files. `patchline_execute` accepts a list of
snapshot-anchored operations and selects exact, Hashline, recoverable batch, or
standard-tool fallback execution when `strategy` is `auto`. Precision mutations
require a snapshot returned by `read`; explicit `strategy: "standard"` routes
without a snapshot or a precision payload. Large replacements return metadata
with `strategy: "standard"`, `nextTool: "apply_patch"`, and zero writes.
The ordinary OpenCode `apply_patch` is not overridden or blocked by precision
mode. Use it for large files, large changes, or unsupported precision operations.
`patchline_apply_patch` handles snapshot-tagged Hashline sections and optional
classic new-file fallback. Native patch attempts conservatively invalidate
Patchline snapshots before and after execution, including partial failures.
The adaptive tool never bypasses the existing edit/write safety services.
Additional tools are `patchline_grep`,
`patchline_lsp`, `ast_search`, `patchline_edit_batch`, and
`patchline_diagnostics`.

Outputs are bounded and include no unchanged full file. Fallback outputs are
compact and do not include full old/new content. Errors contain a stable code
and a corrective action. Successful tool results expose bounded structured
metadata where the OpenCode adapter supports it: `status` (`observed` or
`applied`), `recoveryAction`, and operation-specific fields such as `snapshot`,
`bytesWritten` (actual UTF-8 bytes committed), `bytesRendered`, `added`, `deleted`, `created`, and `validation`. The existing
human-readable output remains available, but consumers should use metadata for
recovery decisions. Mutation tools expose the same validation states:
`not_configured`, `passed`, or `failed`; validation failure does not change an
already-applied mutation into a zero-write result. Mutation cancellation is
propagated from OpenCode and partial cancellation reports rollback details.

Compact `edit` and `patchline_edit_batch` append an already-computed display
diff to their human-readable summaries when it is complete and at most 2,000
characters per file. Oversized or incomplete previews are omitted with an
explicit notice rather than clipped inside a hunk. The aggregate response
retains the 20,000-character output budget; validation failures precede summaries
and previews. Previews are omitted altogether on failed validation or when their
combined summaries and previews exceed 19,000 characters, reserving room for
diagnostic status and preventing aggregate truncation inside a hunk.
Display context does not grant observed-line edit rights and does
not replace stale, identity, preservation or validation checks. Extended output
is unchanged. This preview is a usability change, not evidence of fewer model
reads or provider tokens.

File reads reject files larger than 8 MiB before loading them and reject a
requested range containing a line longer than 20,000 characters before creating
a snapshot. This prevents line-oriented snapshots and tool output from becoming
unbounded while preserving complete text for accepted files. They also reject a
rendered file page above 20,000 characters before recording a snapshot.

Directory reads reject directories with more than 4,096 entries before producing
a paginated result, and reject a page whose rendered output exceeds 20,000
characters. Pagination does not imply unbounded directory enumeration or output.

`write` and exact/Hashline edits reject an output larger than 8 MiB before any
filesystem mutation. A create batch has the same 8 MiB aggregate budget and
preflights that budget before its first file is created. Create batches also
reject more than 500 files before path resolution or filesystem mutation.
Edit batches reject more than 500 edits before snapshot or path preflight.
Successful create and edit batch reports are capped at 20,000 characters with an
explicit truncation marker; output truncation does not change mutation success.

`patchline_diagnostics` requests the OpenCode `bash` permission for the exact
command before execution. Configured post-edit validation commands request the
same permission after a successful edit and before they run. A denied request
prevents the command from starting.

`patchline_grep` treats `pattern` as case-sensitive literal text. Regular
expression semantics are intentionally not part of this tool contract; use AST
search for structural patterns and LSP for symbol relationships. Its optional
`path` may identify either a workspace-relative file or directory; a file path
limits the search to that file. Only valid UTF-8 text files are searched;
invalid UTF-8 and NUL-containing binary files are skipped rather than decoded
with replacement characters or returned as false matches. `include` globs use
`*` for one path segment and `**/` for zero or more directory segments.
Search result limits are validated at the service boundary and must be integers
from 1 through 500. Files larger than 8 MiB are skipped before their content is
loaded, including files that grow past the limit while being read. Each returned
matching-line preview is capped at 2,000 characters. Each enumerated directory is
bounded to 4,096 entries before literal search continues. Directory entries are
sorted by name before traversal so match order is deterministic and independent
of filesystem readdir order. Formatted grep and AST responses remain bounded at 20,000 characters and are
truncated with an actionable narrowing hint. Grep results report skipped-file
counts and bounded reasons for unreadable, unsupported-encoding, binary, or
oversized files.

`patchline_apply_patch` accepts snapshot-tagged Hashline sections for existing files. It
rejects non-whitespace content before the first Hashline section before asking
for edit permission. It
also accepts classic `*** Add File` sections after preflighting that every path
is new when `applyPatchFallback` is enabled. Classic update and delete sections
are rejected. The classic format requires exactly one `*** Begin Patch` / `***
End Patch` envelope and rejects non-whitespace trailing content before any file
is created. Patch input is limited to 8 MiB before parsing or permission requests.
`patchline_summary` is registered only when `summary` is enabled.

`patchline_lsp` passes query and file arguments directly to the installed
OpenCode executable without shell interpretation. On Windows it resolves the
native `opencode.exe` from `PATH` and never invokes the `opencode.cmd` wrapper
through a shell.

# Validation Routing

Status: Accepted

Level 1 performs snapshot and syntax checks. Level 2 selects a changed-file
lint, typecheck, or targeted test command. Level 3 runs affected package tests
or build for larger tasks. Project-wide suites are not run after every local
edit.

# Patchline Visualization Contract

Status: Accepted

Native patch context mismatches follow `native-patch-recovery.md`. Route reasons
and failure reasons have separate fields; the failure is shown once, with native
details disclosed on demand. Single native context failures are patch rejections,
not generic batch failures. Unknown native write counts remain unknown.

Patchline ships both the server (`./server`) and OpenCode TUI (`./tui`) entrypoints
in one npm package. The OpenCode package installer discovers both entrypoints.
After installation or configuration changes, restart OpenCode.
`smoke:install` verifies discovery of both entrypoints through the installed
OpenCode CLI, using an isolated home and XDG/config directories.

The `edit` tool returns a bounded unified `metadata.diff` for OpenCode's native
edit renderer. `apply_patch` returns `metadata.files` in OpenCode's native patch
shape (`type`, `filePath`, `relativePath`, `patch`, `deletions`). Batch edits
return one diff per changed file, with a 20,000-character aggregate preview
budget. Only complete hunks are included; `diffTruncated: true` explicitly marks
omitted content (including an empty preview). Diff computation has a 100 ms /
2,000-edit-distance budget. Exact additions/deletions include blank lines and
are independent of preview limits. Preview text is display-only and must never
be used as an edit source or as proof that a commit succeeded.

Tools report permission, planning, preflight, committing, rollback, validation,
fallback and completion through `ToolContext.metadata`. `patchline_execute` is
rendered as a mutation activity. When the selected strategy is `exact`, the
activity is labelled `Planning exact edit` during planning and reports
`strategy: "exact"`. Large-change standard-tool delegation is rendered as a
compact fallback card with its route reason and recovery action. Presentation
Conversation slots include `patchline_execute` and `patchline_apply_patch`.
Adaptive Hashline results expose the same bounded file diffs as batch edits.
callbacks cannot stop a commit or rollback. Thrown errors remain rejected tool
calls with a reason, recovery action, stage, paths and write count where known.
`writes` counts landed file writes, including subsequently restored files;
`restored` and `conflicts` identify rollback outcomes. Unknown commit outcomes
never imply zero writes.
A nonzero validation exit retains `status: applied` with `validation: failed`;
a validation exception retains the applied diff, snapshot and `writes: 1` in
error metadata. Hashline batch metadata includes all source and move paths;
`REM`/`MV` failures expose the same landed-write and rollback conflict fields.
Both are shown as applied changes with failed validation.

Patchline does not register a sidebar activity slot. Tool activity cards appear
in the conversation and use the active OpenCode theme. Mutation
operations (`edit`, `write`, `apply_patch`, `patchline_edit_batch`) show writes,
validation, additions, deletions and bounded file previews. Read, search, route,
LSP, diagnostics and summary tools expose the same activity card with a
structured operation-specific summary.

Activity panels follow the host tool style: themed panel background, a left
accent, horizontal padding, one row of internal padding above/below content,
and external top/bottom separation from adjacent conversation content.
Paths appear directly below the operation heading, before secondary metadata.
Completed mutation diffs are collapsed by default, but changed-file headers
and their theme-colored addition/deletion counts always remain visible.
Card and file headings are not disclosure controls. English footer actions
(`Show details ↓` / `Hide details ↑`, `Show file ↓` / `Hide file ↑`) toggle
details and individual files independently. Selecting text must not toggle
previews. A blank row separates each card heading from its summary. The left
border and status indicator use theme warning while running, success after
completion, and error on failure, independently of disclosure state.
Text results initially show twelve lines and reveal twelve more per footer
action; `Show fewer lines ↑` restores the initial preview. Results retain the
20,000-character display-only bound and explicitly mark omitted content.
Diffs initially show one complete hunk; footer controls reveal subsequent
changes and restore the first-hunk preview without cutting unified-diff hunks.
Expanded view uses OpenTUI's native `diff` renderer in unified mode with
monospace code, syntax highlighting when the file type is known, line numbers,
hunk headers, plus/minus signs, and the current theme's added/removed/context
backgrounds and sign colors. Errors show recovery details; diff disclosure
remains under the same footer controls. Session counters use aligned English
labels and values rather than raw camelCase keys.

Its animated indicator runs only during an operation and stops on completion or
unmount. TUI JSX is compiled with Solid's universal transform so theme, tool
state and expanded state remain reactive. `smoke:tui` requires Bun and mounts
the compiled entrypoint in the native OpenTUI test renderer; it checks
transitions, animation, interactive expansion, native diff rendering,
validation failures, rollback details and disposal.

The TUI view is bounded to four files and the existing aggregate diff preview
budget. It reads only existing tool-part metadata; it does not poll the
filesystem or keep a second copy of snapshots. Preview text is display-only.

## Conversation renderer host extension

Stock OpenCode 1.18.34 does not expose tool-card slots. Conversation rendering
requires the modified host checkout `.opencode-host/` (ignored by Git).
Its session `ToolPart` wraps the existing tool switch in a replacement slot
named `tool_<tool ID>`, passing reactive `part`, `message` and `last` props.
Unregistered slots retain the existing renderer. Patchline registers its tool

Launch `.opencode-host/packages/opencode/dist/opencode-windows-x64/bin/opencode.exe`

`PATCHLINE_HOST_SMOKE=1` and run `npm run smoke:tui` to load the actual host

# Write Guard Contract

Status: Accepted

New files may be created. Existing source files must be changed through
snapshot-anchored `edit`. Existing generated files require their canonical
generator. Explicit full replacement is an opt-in allowlist exception and does
not bypass path safety. Missing parent directories are created component by
component with canonical and identity checks; only operation-owned empty
directories may be cleaned up after a failed create.

# Cross-Platform Testing

CI must cover Windows, Linux, and macOS. Platform cases include drive letters,
POSIX roots, case behavior, LF/CRLF, BOM, Unicode, spaces, symlinks, and Git
worktrees. Tests must not assume POSIX shell syntax.

# Fixture Policy

Fixtures cover LF, CRLF, BOM, Unicode names, spaces, large files, generated
artifacts, symlinks, and separate worktrees. Preservation assertions compare
raw bytes and changed-line counts, not only decoded strings.

# Integration Testing

Integration tests use temporary workspaces and invoke service/tool contracts
through real filesystem adapters. OpenCode package loading and at least one
native LSP are smoke-tested when the matching runtime is available.

# Stale Edit Scenarios

Required cases are unchanged source, changes before/after/inside the target,
target deletion, file deletion, rename, concurrent edit, and one stale member
of a multi-file batch. Every stale case expects zero intended writes.

# Test Strategy

P0 uses unit and filesystem integration tests for snapshots, stale mutation,
exact and anchored edits, write guards, path safety, encoding, line endings,
large files, and multi-file preflight. P1 adds search, diagnostics, plugin hook,
and real runtime smoke tests. Every regression receives a failing test first.

# HTML Report Format The architectural review is rendered as a single self-contained HTML file in the OS temp directory. Tailwind and Mermaid both come from CDNs. Mermaid handles graph-shaped diagrams reliably; hand-built divs and inline SVG handle the more editorial visuals (mass diagrams, cross-sections). Mix the two: don't lean on Mermaid for everything, it'll start to look generic. ## Scaffold ```html Architecture review for {{repo name}}
...
...
...
``` ## Header Repo name, date, and a compact legend: solid box = module, dashed line = seam, red arrow = leakage, thick dark box = deep module. No introduction paragraph. Straight into the candidates. ## Candidate card The diagrams carry the weight. Prose is sparse, plain, and uses the glossary terms (from the `/codebase-design` skill) without ceremony. Each candidate is one `
`: - **Title**: short, names the deepening (e.g. "Collapse the Order intake pipeline"). - **Badge row**: recommendation strength (`Strong` = emerald, `Worth exploring` = amber, `Speculative` = slate), plus a tag for the dependency category (`in-process`, `local-substitutable`, `ports & adapters`, `mock`). - **Files**: monospaced list, `font-mono text-sm`. - **Before / After diagram**: the centrepiece. Two columns, side by side. See patterns below. - **Problem**: one sentence. What hurts. - **Solution**: one sentence. What changes. - **Wins**: bullets, ≤6 words each. e.g. "Tests hit one interface", "Pricing logic stops leaking", "Delete 4 shallow wrappers". - **ADR callout** (if applicable): one line in an amber-tinted box. No paragraphs of explanation. If the diagram needs a paragraph to be understood, redraw the diagram. ## Diagram patterns Pick the pattern that fits the candidate. Mix them. Don't make every diagram look the same. Variety is part of the point. ### Mermaid graph (the workhorse for dependencies / call flow) Use a Mermaid `flowchart` or `graph` when the point is "X calls Y calls Z, and look at the mess." Wrap it in a Tailwind-styled card so it doesn't feel parachuted in. Style with classDef to colour leakage edges red and the deep module dark. Sequence diagrams work well for "before: 6 round-trips; after: 1." ```html 
    flowchart LR
      A[OrderHandler] --> B[OrderValidator]
      B --> C[OrderRepo]
      C -.leak.-> D[PricingClient]
      classDef leak stroke:#dc2626,stroke-width:2px;
      class C,D leak
``` ### Hand-built boxes-and-arrows (when Mermaid's layout fights you) Modules as `
`s with borders and labels. Arrows as inline SVG `` or `` elements positioned absolutely over a relative container. Reach for this when you want the "after" diagram to feel like one thick-bordered deep module with greyed-out internals, since Mermaid won't render that with the right weight. ### Cross-section (good for layered shallowness) Stack horizontal bands (`h-12 border-l-4`) to show layers a call passes through. Before: 6 thin layers each doing nothing. After: 1 thick band labelled with the consolidated responsibility. ### Mass diagram (good for "interface as wide as implementation") Two rectangles per module: one for interface surface area, one for implementation. Before: interface rectangle is nearly as tall as the implementation rectangle (shallow). After: interface rectangle is short, implementation rectangle is tall (deep). ### Call-graph collapse Before: a tree of function calls rendered as nested boxes. After: the same tree collapsed into one box, with the now-internal calls shown faded inside it. ## Style guidance - Lean editorial, not corporate-dashboard. Generous whitespace. Serif optional for headings (`font-serif` works well with stone/slate). - Colour sparingly: one accent (emerald or indigo) plus red for leakage and amber for warnings. - Keep diagrams ~320px tall so before/after sits comfortably side by side without scrolling. - Use `text-xs uppercase tracking-wider` for module labels inside diagrams, so they read as schematic, not as UI. - The only scripts are the Tailwind CDN and the Mermaid ESM import. The report is otherwise static: no app code, no interactivity beyond Mermaid's own rendering. ## Top recommendation section One larger card. Candidate name, one sentence on why, anchor link to its card. That's it. ## Tone Plain English, concise, but the architectural nouns and verbs come straight from the `/codebase-design` skill. Concision is not an excuse to drift. **Use exactly:** module, interface, implementation, depth, deep, shallow, seam, adapter, leverage, locality. **Never substitute:** component, service, unit (for module) · API, signature (for interface) · boundary (for seam) · layer, wrapper (for module, when you mean module). **Phrasings that fit the style:** - "Order intake module is shallow: interface nearly matches the implementation." - "Pricing leaks across the seam." - "Deepen: one interface, one place to test." - "Two adapters justify the seam: HTTP in prod, in-memory in tests." **Wins bullets** name the gain in glossary terms: *"locality: bugs concentrate in one module"*, *"leverage: one interface, N call sites"*, *"interface shrinks; implementation absorbs the wrappers"*. Don't write *"easier to maintain"* or *"cleaner code"*, because those terms aren't in the glossary and don't earn their place. No hedging, no throat-clearing, no "it's worth noting that…". If a sentence could be a bullet, make it a bullet. If a bullet could be cut, cut it. If a term isn't in the `/codebase-design` glossary, reach for one that is before inventing a new one.

# Creation Log: Systematic Debugging Skill

Reference example of extracting, structuring, and bulletproofing a critical skill.

## Source Material

Extracted debugging framework from `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`:
- 4-phase systematic process (Investigation → Pattern Analysis → Hypothesis → Implementation)
- Core mandate: ALWAYS find root cause, NEVER fix symptoms
- Rules designed to resist time pressure and rationalization

## Extraction Decisions

**What to include:**
- Complete 4-phase framework with all rules
- Anti-shortcuts ("NEVER fix symptom", "STOP and re-analyze")
- Pressure-resistant language ("even if faster", "even if I seem in a hurry")
- Concrete steps for each phase

**What to leave out:**
- Project-specific context
- Repetitive variations of same rule
- Narrative explanations (condensed to principles)

## Structure Following skill-creation/SKILL.md

1. **Rich when_to_use** - Included symptoms and anti-patterns
2. **Type: technique** - Concrete process with steps
3. **Keywords** - "root cause", "symptom", "workaround", "debugging", "investigation"
4. **Flowchart** - Decision point for "fix failed" → re-analyze vs add more fixes
5. **Phase-by-phase breakdown** - Scannable checklist format
6. **Anti-patterns section** - What NOT to do (critical for this skill)

## Bulletproofing Elements

Framework designed to resist rationalization under pressure:

### Language Choices
- "ALWAYS" / "NEVER" (not "should" / "try to")
- "even if faster" / "even if I seem in a hurry"
- "STOP and re-analyze" (explicit pause)
- "Don't skip past" (catches the actual behavior)

### Structural Defenses
- **Phase 1 required** - Can't skip to implementation
- **Single hypothesis rule** - Forces thinking, prevents shotgun fixes
- **Explicit failure mode** - "IF your first fix doesn't work" with mandatory action
- **Anti-patterns section** - Shows exactly what shortcuts look like

### Redundancy
- Root cause mandate in overview + when_to_use + Phase 1 + implementation rules
- "NEVER fix symptom" appears 4 times in different contexts
- Each phase has explicit "don't skip" guidance

## Testing Approach

Created 4 validation tests following skills/meta/testing-skills-with-subagents:

### Test 1: Academic Context (No Pressure)
- Simple bug, no time pressure
- **Result:** Perfect compliance, complete investigation

### Test 2: Time Pressure + Obvious Quick Fix
- User "in a hurry", symptom fix looks easy
- **Result:** Resisted shortcut, followed full process, found real root cause

### Test 3: Complex System + Uncertainty
- Multi-layer failure, unclear if can find root cause
- **Result:** Systematic investigation, traced through all layers, found source

### Test 4: Failed First Fix
- Hypothesis doesn't work, temptation to add more fixes
- **Result:** Stopped, re-analyzed, formed new hypothesis (no shotgun)

**All tests passed.** No rationalizations found.

## Iterations

### Initial Version
- Complete 4-phase framework
- Anti-patterns section
- Flowchart for "fix failed" decision

### Enhancement 1: TDD Reference
- Added link to skills/testing/test-driven-development
- Note explaining TDD's "simplest code" ≠ debugging's "root cause"
- Prevents confusion between methodologies

## Final Outcome

Bulletproof skill that:
- ✅ Clearly mandates root cause investigation
- ✅ Resists time pressure rationalization
- ✅ Provides concrete steps for each phase
- ✅ Shows anti-patterns explicitly
- ✅ Tested under multiple pressure scenarios
- ✅ Clarifies relationship to TDD
- ✅ Ready for use

## Key Insight

**Most important bulletproofing:** Anti-patterns section showing exact shortcuts that feel justified in the moment. When Claude thinks "I'll just add this one quick fix", seeing that exact pattern listed as wrong creates cognitive friction.

## Usage Example

When encountering a bug:
1. Load skill: skills/debugging/systematic-debugging
2. Read overview (10 sec) - reminded of mandate
3. Follow Phase 1 checklist - forced investigation
4. If tempted to skip - see anti-pattern, stop
5. Complete all phases - root cause found

**Time investment:** 5-10 minutes
**Time saved:** Hours of symptom-whack-a-mole

# Writing Good Tests

**Load this reference when:** writing or changing tests, adding mocks, or
adding cleanup/helper methods for tests.

## Overview

A test exists to catch a specific break. Two principles govern everything
here:

```
1. Every test names the break it catches
2. Every test exercises the real thing
```

Strict TDD produces both naturally: a test written first and watched
failing against real code has already proven it can fail, and only earns
a mock when the real dependency proves slow or external.

## Principle 1: Name the Break

Before writing the test body, answer: **what production change should
make this test fail — and is that change a bug or a decision?** A test
earns its place by catching a wrong branch, missing side effect, wrong
argument, boundary case, or broken contract.

**Derive expectations independently.** Use literals and hand-checked
fixtures; table-driven tests with literal `want` values are the preferred
shape. An expectation computed by the code under test — or its helpers
…[内容超出评审预算——仅保留首尾各 1024 字符]…
s side effects; mock the slow/external level |
| Build a mock response | Mirror the real structure completely |
| Need cleanup only tests use | Put it in test utilities |
| Watch mock setup balloon | Switch to an integration test with real components |
| Finish a test file | Run the mutation check |

## Warning Signs

- Setup and assertion share the same object, guaranteeing equality
- The test can fail only through a panic, crash, or missing selector
- The test fails on every intentional change, never on accidental breakage
- Expected values are hidden behind loops, builders, or helpers
- The test greps source text, or asserts a removed symbol stays removed
- The test would still matter if only the framework remained
- The test exists for coverage, checking no side effect or outcome
- An assertion checks a `*-mock` test ID, or fails if you remove the mock
- A method is called only from test files
- Mock setup is more than half the test, or you can't explain why the mock is needed
- Mocking "just to be safe"
